ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:

    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))

title: Introduction to Bitcoin: chapter 1 of the 3rd edition, with its terms explained and its figures recomputed

nodes.label: Money
nodes.body: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Money branch gathers everything the chapter says about that currency itself: what its unit is called and how the unit is divided, how much of it will ever exist, who creates it and when, and what decides its price.

paras.text: Chapter 1 begins by saying that Bitcoin is a collection of concepts and technologies that form the basis of a digital money ecosystem, and that units of currency called bitcoin are used to store and transmit value among the participants of the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Money branch gathers everything the chapter says about that currency itself: what its unit is called and how the unit is divided, how much of it will ever exist, who creates it and when, and what decides its price.

A currency is only as useful as the rules that govern it. People accept money because they expect to be able to spend it later at a value they can foresee, and the expectation depends on knowing who can create more of it and how fast. Conventional currencies answer these questions with institutions, namely a central bank and a clearing system, whereas Bitcoin answers them with rules written into software that every participant can read. Understanding the monetary side first makes the technical machinery of the later branches easier to follow, because every mechanism exists to protect one of these monetary rules.

The monetary rules appear in every part of the chapter. The unit and its subdivisions appear whenever Alice and Joe agree on an amount. The supply schedule appears in the account of mining, where new bitcoin is paid out as a reward. The price appears in the section that asks who sets the price of bitcoin, and the issuance rules appear in the argument that mining replaces the functions of a central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has four sections. The Unit section fixes the vocabulary of bitcoin, the satoshi and the capital letter. The Supply section explains the schedule by which the total supply stays just below 21 million and how the subsidy of each block is halved at fixed intervals. The Price section explains why the exchange rate floats and how a single market rate is computed from many trades. The Issuance section compares Bitcoin's way of creating money with that of a central bank and explains why the currency is called deflationary.

Three misconceptions are worth removing early. First, there is no company or authority that issues bitcoin; the rules of issuance are enforced by every participant. Second, the number of bitcoin is not unlimited, but the limit is a property of the software rules and not a law of nature, so it is only as strong as the agreement of the participants to keep it. Third, a figure such as the price or the current subsidy is a value at a date; the chapter's rules stay fixed while those values change.

nodes.label: Unit
nodes.body: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi. Together these give a student the exact vocabulary in which amounts are written in the rest of the course (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Unit section answers the first question that any money raises, namely what the money is called and in what pieces it is counted. It contains the name of the currency, with its distinction between the unit and the system, and the smallest subdivision that can be recorded, the satoshi. Together these give a student the exact vocabulary in which amounts are written in the rest of the course (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

An imprecise vocabulary produces imprecise reasoning. A student who writes that Bitcoin was sent when bitcoin was meant has confused the payment system with the thing that it transports, and an engineer who forgets how amounts are divided will make rounding errors in software that handles real value. The unit section therefore comes first so that every later figure can be stated without ambiguity.

The two concepts of this section move from the name to the arithmetic. The first one explains the convention of writing bitcoin with a small letter for the unit and Bitcoin with a capital letter for the system. The second one explains the satoshi, the integer unit in which amounts are counted, and shows with a short computation how a decimal amount of bitcoin is converted into satoshis exactly.

nodes.label: Bitcoin unit
nodes.body: Bitcoin is the name of the system, and bitcoin is the name of the unit of currency that the system transports. The book states the convention in a short note: the unit of currency is called bitcoin with a small b, and the system is called Bitcoin with a capital B (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The abbreviation BTC stands for the unit, as in the amount 0.001 BTC that Joe sends to Alice and in the currency pair BTC/USD that is used to quote its price in United States dollars.

paras.text: Bitcoin is the name of the system, and bitcoin is the name of the unit of currency that the system transports. The book states the convention in a short note: the unit of currency is called bitcoin with a small b, and the system is called Bitcoin with a capital B (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The abbreviation BTC stands for the unit, as in the amount 0.001 BTC that Joe sends to Alice and in the currency pair BTC/USD that is used to quote its price in United States dollars.

The distinction is more than a matter of spelling. The system consists of a protocol, a network, and software, while the unit is a quantity of value that is recorded by that system. Chapter 1 describes the unit as a currency that is entirely virtual, since there are no physical coins and not even individual digital coins, and it describes the system as a collection of concepts and technologies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Keeping the two words apart prevents sentences such as a Bitcoin was sent, which blur the difference between the thing that moves and the machinery that moves it.

A reader meets the unit whenever an amount is written. Wallets show balances in BTC, exchanges quote prices in pairs such as BTC/USD, and the examples of this chapter use amounts such as 0.001 BTC. The system, by contrast, is named when someone speaks of the Bitcoin network, the Bitcoin protocol or Bitcoin users. The same capital-letter convention is followed by the textbook throughout, and the course materials follow it as well.

The unit is divisible. The chapter notes that some wallets show an amount in a different denomination, because 0.001 BTC is 1 millibitcoin (mBTC) or 100,000 satoshis (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet may therefore show the same quantity in several units, and none of the displays changes the amount itself. The next concept, the satoshi, explains the smallest of these units and gives the arithmetic that relates them.

A common slip is to treat bitcoin as a physical or digital object that can be held in the way that a coin can. The chapter is explicit that coins are implied in transactions that transfer value from spender to receiver, and that no coin object exists (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second slip is to write bitcoin with a capital letter in the middle of a sentence when the unit is meant. The convention is a convention of this textbook; other writers do not always follow it, so a student should read an unfamiliar text with the possibility of a different usage in mind.

nodes.label: Satoshi (unit)
nodes.body: A satoshi is the smallest denomination of bitcoin that can be recorded on the blockchain. It equals 0.00000001 bitcoin, that is, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, and it is named after Satoshi Nakamoto, the person or people who designed Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word is often shortened to sat. In this text the word satoshi with a small s always means this unit, while the capitalised name Satoshi Nakamoto means the author of the whitepaper, which is a separate concept of the History section.

paras.text: A satoshi is the smallest denomination of bitcoin that can be recorded on the blockchain. It equals 0.00000001 bitcoin, that is, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, and it is named after Satoshi Nakamoto, the person or people who designed Bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word is often shortened to sat. In this text the word satoshi with a small s always means this unit, while the capitalised name Satoshi Nakamoto means the author of the whitepaper, which is a separate concept of the History section.

A currency that is divided into very small pieces can be used for very small payments, and a system that counts in whole units avoids a class of errors. Software represents an amount as an integer number of satoshis, because integers add and subtract exactly, whereas decimal fractions held in floating-point numbers do not always do so. Bitcoin Core, the reference implementation, defines one bitcoin as 100,000,000 of its smallest units and uses a whole-number amount type for the value of every output (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The chapter meets the satoshi in the Alice and Joe example. When Joe enters the amount of 0.001 bitcoin, the text remarks that some wallets will show the amount in a different denomination: 0.001 BTC is 1 millibitcoin (mBTC) or 100,000 satoshis (sats) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets for everyday payments often show amounts in satoshis, because a whole number of satoshis is easier to read than a decimal fraction of a bitcoin with many leading zeros.

The conversion is a multiplication by 10 to the power 8. The computation Decimal('0.001') * 10**8 evaluates to 100000, so 0.001 bitcoin is exactly 100000 satoshis, and the maximum supply of 21 million bitcoin corresponds to 2,100,000,000,000,000 satoshis. The example uses Python's decimal type instead of an ordinary floating-point number on purpose: decimal arithmetic keeps the digits that were typed, so the result is an exact integer. The amount type of Bitcoin Core is an integer count of satoshis, and its limit of 21 million coins is written as 21 million times that count (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two warnings apply. First, the satoshi must not be confused with Satoshi Nakamoto, although the unit is named after the author. Second, a conversion done with ordinary floating-point numbers can be off by a tiny amount, which is harmless in a classroom exercise and dangerous in software that moves value; the safe habit is to convert at the edges of a program and to compute with whole numbers of satoshis in between.

nodes.definition: The satoshi is the smallest unit of bitcoin that can be recorded, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin; amounts are counted in whole satoshis.

nodes.label: Supply
nodes.body: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This section explains the three ideas behind that sentence: the cap on the total, the halving of the subsidy at fixed intervals, and the subsidy itself, which is the amount of new bitcoin paid to the miner of each block.

paras.text: The Supply section is about how much bitcoin exists and how the amount grows. The chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, limiting the total to a fixed number just below 21 million, so that the number in circulation follows a predictable curve (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This section explains the three ideas behind that sentence: the cap on the total, the halving of the subsidy at fixed intervals, and the subsidy itself, which is the amount of new bitcoin paid to the miner of each block.

Predictability is the economic point of the schedule. Anyone can compute in advance how many bitcoin will exist at any future block, and nobody can change the schedule without the agreement of the participants who run the software. For a student, the supply schedule is also the best first example of how a rule of an economic system can be written as a short program and checked by execution.

The three concepts build on one another. The block subsidy is the quantity that is paid for each block. The halving is the rule that cuts the subsidy in half every 210,000 blocks. The supply cap is the total that results when all the subsidies of all the eras are added together, and the section shows that the sum is just below 21 million and not equal to it, because each era's subsidy is a whole number of satoshis.

nodes.label: Supply cap
nodes.body: The supply cap is the upper limit on the total amount of bitcoin that can ever exist. The chapter states it as a fixed total just below 21 million coins, and explains that the number in circulation follows an easily predictable curve in which half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cap is not stored as a single number that is checked; it is a consequence of the rule that fixes how much new bitcoin each block may create.

paras.text: The supply cap is the upper limit on the total amount of bitcoin that can ever exist. The chapter states it as a fixed total just below 21 million coins, and explains that the number in circulation follows an easily predictable curve in which half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cap is not stored as a single number that is checked; it is a consequence of the rule that fixes how much new bitcoin each block may create.

A limit on supply is what distinguishes Bitcoin from a currency that a central bank can expand. Because the rule is enforced by every full node, a miner who tries to claim more than the rule allows produces a block that the other participants reject. The chapter adds that nobody can force you to accept any bitcoins that were created beyond the expected issuance rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cap therefore is a promise about future behaviour that is backed by the participants' own software and not by the word of an issuer.

The cap is met in discussions of the long-term value of bitcoin, in the explanation of why mining rewards shrink, and in the consensus code of Bitcoin Core. There the constant MAX_MONEY is defined as 21 million times the number of satoshis in one bitcoin, and the function that computes the subsidy of a block halves the starting subsidy of 50 bitcoin once for each interval of 210,000 blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Bitcoin Wiki gives the same schedule and adds that the exact total is slightly less than 21 million (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

The subsidy begins at 50 bitcoin per block. After each interval of 210,000 blocks it is shifted right by one binary place, which halves it, and any fraction smaller than one satoshi is dropped. Adding the subsidy of every one of the 33 eras that have a non-zero subsidy gives the total: the expression sum((50 * 10**8 >> era) * 210000 for era in range(33)) / 10**8 evaluates to 20999999.9769 bitcoin. The shortfall of 0.0231 bitcoin below 21 million comes from rounding down to whole satoshis, which the program shows because it works with whole numbers of satoshis. The chapter source also leaves a short script as a comment: it adds 50 divided by 2 to the power of the era number once per block, and the block at which the running total first exceeds 99 percent of 21 million is block 1,411,200, the figure that the chapter quotes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A cap is a rule of the software and not a physical law. It holds as long as the participants who run full nodes continue to enforce it, and changing it would require nearly all of them to agree on new software, which is why the schedule is regarded as stable. A second caution concerns the phrase just below 21 million: the true total is 20999999.9769 bitcoin, so a program that assumes exactly 21,000,000 will be off by a small but real amount. A third caution is that the cap says nothing about coins whose keys are lost; those remain counted in the supply although no one can spend them.

nodes.label: Halving
nodes.body: A halving is the event at which the block subsidy is cut in half. The rule is part of the protocol: the chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, and that half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin Core the interval is a constant, nSubsidyHalvingInterval, whose value for the main network is 210,000 blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

paras.text: A halving is the event at which the block subsidy is cut in half. The rule is part of the protocol: the chapter says that the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, and that half of the remaining coins are added to circulation every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In Bitcoin Core the interval is a constant, nSubsidyHalvingInterval, whose value for the main network is 210,000 blocks (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The halving is the mechanism that makes the supply curve geometric. Each interval pays half as much as the one before, so the total converges to a limit instead of growing without end, and the issuance of new bitcoin becomes less and less important compared with the fees paid by transactions. The halving also changes the economics of mining at fixed dates, because a miner's revenue from new bitcoin drops by half on that day.

A halving is a recurring event in the news and in the history of the network. The first subsidy of 50 bitcoin applied from the first block; the fifth era began at block 840000, which according to the block data from the Blockstream explorer carries the time stamp 1713571767, that is 2024-04-20 00:09:27 UTC, and from that block the subsidy has been 3.125 bitcoin (Blockstream, 2026). The Bitcoin Wiki table of the projected supply lists the same block and date (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

The program divides the block height by 210000 to find the number of halvings that have already happened, and it shifts the initial subsidy of 50 * 10**8 satoshis to the right by that many places. For block 840000 the division gives 4, and the shifted value is 312,500,000 satoshis, which is 3.125 bitcoin. Bitcoin Core computes the subsidy in the same way: it divides the height by the interval, returns zero when the number of halvings is 64 or more because a shift by 64 places would be undefined, and otherwise right-shifts 50 times the number of satoshis in a bitcoin (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The chapter says that a halving happens about every four years, and the text of the course must not state this as an exact calendar fact. The interval is a number of blocks, 210000, and the calendar time depends on how fast blocks are actually found; at the target of one block every 10 minutes it comes to a little less than four years (210000 blocks of 10 minutes each last 3.99 years). The dates of later halvings are therefore estimates until they occur.

nodes.definition: The block subsidy halves every 210000 blocks; at block 840000, on 2024-04-20, it fell to 3.125 bitcoin.

nodes.label: Block subsidy
nodes.body: The block subsidy is the amount of newly created bitcoin that the rules allow the miner of a block to claim. The chapter describes the payment in general terms: on average every 10 minutes one miner can add security to past transactions, and is rewarded with both brand new bitcoins and the fees paid by recent transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The new bitcoins are the subsidy, and the fees are the second part of the miner's reward.

paras.text: The block subsidy is the amount of newly created bitcoin that the rules allow the miner of a block to claim. The chapter describes the payment in general terms: on average every 10 minutes one miner can add security to past transactions, and is rewarded with both brand new bitcoins and the fees paid by recent transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The new bitcoins are the subsidy, and the fees are the second part of the miner's reward.

The subsidy is the only way in which new bitcoin enters circulation, so it is at once the supply policy and the payment for the work of securing the network. The whitepaper explains the design: the first transaction in a block is a special transaction that starts a new coin owned by the creator of the block, which adds an incentive for nodes to support the network and provides a way to distribute coins into circulation in the absence of a central authority (Nakamoto, 2008). The same paper compares the steady addition of coins with gold miners who expend resources to add gold to circulation.

Every block carries the subsidy in its first transaction, and every full node checks it. Bitcoin Core compares the value paid by that transaction with the sum of the transaction fees of the block and the subsidy computed from the block height, and it rejects the block if the miner has claimed more (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Block explorers and wallets that display a block's reward show the sum of the subsidy and the fees.

The subsidy depends only on the block height. Starting from 50 bitcoin it is halved once for every 210,000 blocks, so the list of subsidies at the first block of each of five eras is 50.0, 25.0, 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 bitcoin. The result of the expression that appears in the example can be reproduced for any height with the same two operations, a division and a shift. Because the subsidy is a function of height alone, every node reaches the same value without exchanging a message.

The subsidy is not the same as the reward: the reward of a block is the subsidy plus the fees of its transactions, and the glossary of the book describes the reward as the amount included in each new block for the miner who found the proof of work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The figure in that glossary entry, 12.5 bitcoin, was the subsidy at the time the glossary was written and is out of date. Because the subsidy keeps halving, the fees become a larger share of the reward over time, a development the whitepaper anticipated when it says that the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees (Nakamoto, 2008).

nodes.definition: The block subsidy is the amount of new bitcoin that a block may create for its miner; it starts at 50 bitcoin and halves every 210000 blocks.

nodes.label: Price
nodes.body: The Price section addresses a question that every newcomer asks, namely who sets the price of bitcoin. The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The section contains the idea of a floating exchange rate and the way in which a single quotation is computed from the many trades that happen in different places.

The chapter's short answer is that the price is set by markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The section contains the idea of a floating exchange rate and the way in which a single quotation is computed from the many trades that happen in different places.

Bitcoin has no issuer who could announce a price, and it has no central bank that could fix an exchange rate against another currency. The price therefore has to be discovered, and the quality of the discovery determines whether two people can agree on how much cash is worth a given amount of bitcoin, as Alice and Joe must before their exchange.

The first concept in the section explains why the rate floats and how it is quoted as a currency pair. The second concept explains the volume-weighted average, the statistic that pricing services use to combine the prices of several markets into one figure, and gives a small computation that shows why a trade of large volume counts for more than a trade of small volume.

nodes.label: Floating exchange rate
nodes.body: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and a floating exchange rate is one that is not fixed by any authority but moves according to the demand for the currencies and the amount available. The chapter states that Bitcoin, like most other currencies, has a floating exchange rate, which means that the value of bitcoin fluctuates according to supply and demand in the various markets where it is traded (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and a floating exchange rate is one that is not fixed by any authority but moves according to the demand for the currencies and the amount available. The chapter states that Bitcoin, like most other currencies, has a floating exchange rate, which means that the value of bitcoin fluctuates according to supply and demand in the various markets where it is traded (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The explanation answers the question of who sets the price: markets do. This matters for anyone who accepts bitcoin as payment, because the value of the amount received can change between the moment of the agreement and the moment the money is spent. It also explains why the chapter treats the price as an input that Alice and Joe must look up before every exchange, and not as a property of the network itself.

A rate is always written as a pair of currencies, such as BTC/USD, which gives the number of United States dollars for one bitcoin. The chapter notes that the price in dollars is calculated in each market from the most recent trade, so that it tends to fluctuate minutely several times per second, and that pricing services aggregate several markets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Many wallets convert amounts between bitcoin and other currencies automatically by using such a rate.

The conversion itself is a multiplication. If the rate were 60,000 dollars per bitcoin, the amount of 0.001 bitcoin that Alice buys would be worth 0.001 * 60000, which evaluates to 60.0 dollars. The rate used in the example is invented for illustration, and no claim is made about any real price; the point is that the same amount of bitcoin is worth a different number of dollars whenever the rate changes.

A floating rate is not an error or a defect; it is the ordinary condition of most currencies, and the chapter says so. The risk is the volatility that comes with it, so a merchant who prices goods in a national currency but accepts bitcoin must convert at the moment of sale. A further caution concerns the data: the price shown by one website is the price of one market or one average, and two services may differ slightly, which the next concept explains.

nodes.definition: The price of bitcoin is set by markets: a floating exchange rate that moves with supply and demand.

nodes.label: Volume-weighted average
nodes.body: A volume-weighted average is an average of prices in which each price counts in proportion to the volume traded at that price. The chapter says that a pricing service will aggregate the prices from several markets and calculate a volume-weighted average representing the broad market exchange rate of a currency pair, for example BTC/USD (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Bitcoin Average service that the book lists as its first example provides a view of the volume-weighted average for each currency.

paras.text: A volume-weighted average is an average of prices in which each price counts in proportion to the volume traded at that price. The chapter says that a pricing service will aggregate the prices from several markets and calculate a volume-weighted average representing the broad market exchange rate of a currency pair, for example BTC/USD (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Bitcoin Average service that the book lists as its first example provides a view of the volume-weighted average for each currency.

A simple average treats a trade of one small unit and a trade of a thousand units as equal, so a single small and unusual trade could move the result. Weighting by volume makes the figure reflect where most of the money actually changed hands. The result is a more stable and more representative reference rate, which is why pricing services and institutional reference rates use this kind of average (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Services that publish a market price for bitcoin, such as the ones named in the chapter, combine many trading venues into a single quotation. The chapter lists Bitcoin Average, CoinCap and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange Bitcoin Reference Rate, which it describes as a rate that can be used for institutional and contractual reference (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Wallets that display amounts in a national currency obtain such a quotation from a service of this kind.

The computation multiplies each price by its volume, adds the products, and divides by the total volume. If three units traded at the price 100 and one unit traded at the price 104, the weighted average is (100 * 3 + 104 * 1) / 4, which the expression in the example evaluates to 101.0, while the simple average of the two prices would be 102.0. The result lies closer to 100 because the larger trade has the larger weight.

The average is a summary and not a market price that anybody can necessarily trade at. Its value depends on which markets a service includes and on the period over which the trades are collected, so two services can report different numbers for the same currency pair. A volume-weighted average can also lag a fast-moving market, because older trades remain in the window; a person who needs to buy at a specific moment must look at the actual offers on the market where the purchase takes place.

nodes.example: two trades, 3 units at 100 and 1 unit at 104
nodes.definition: A volume-weighted average prices a currency pair by weighting each trade's price by its volume, so larger trades count for more.

nodes.label: Issuance
nodes.body: The Issuance section is about who creates money and by what rule. In a conventional economy a central bank controls the creation of money, and a clearing system settles payments between banks. The chapter argues that Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank, and it describes the currency as deflationary over the long term (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Issuance section is about who creates money and by what rule. In a conventional economy a central bank controls the creation of money, and a clearing system settles payments between banks. The chapter argues that Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank, and it describes the currency as deflationary over the long term (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Issuance is the point at which Bitcoin differs most from the money that students already know. A central bank can respond to an emergency by creating more money, and a clearing house can reverse or delay a payment, but a rule-based system gives up both powers in exchange for predictability and for independence from any single institution. The section helps a student to judge that trade-off with the institutions in front of him.

The four concepts of the section pair the old with the new. The central bank and the clearing house are the institutions that the chapter says Bitcoin replaces. The replacement concept describes how mining takes over their functions, and the deflation concept describes the long-term consequence of an issuance that shrinks until it ends, with a computed date for the last subsidy.

nodes.label: Central bank
nodes.body: A central bank is an institution that issues a country's currency and controls how much of it is created. The Bitcoin Wiki describes the arrangement in a centralized economy: currency is issued by a central bank at a rate that is supposed to match the growth of the amount of goods that are exchanged, so that these goods can be traded with stable prices, and the monetary base is controlled by that bank (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

paras.text: A central bank is an institution that issues a country's currency and controls how much of it is created. The Bitcoin Wiki describes the arrangement in a centralized economy: currency is issued by a central bank at a rate that is supposed to match the growth of the amount of goods that are exchanged, so that these goods can be traded with stable prices, and the monetary base is controlled by that bank (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

The concept is needed in this chapter because the chapter defines Bitcoin partly by contrast. It says that Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student who does not know what a central bank does cannot judge the claim, so the function has to be named: creation of money by an authority, according to a policy that the authority can change.

The everyday example is the central bank of a country. The Bitcoin Wiki names the United States central bank and says that it increases the monetary base by issuing currency, by increasing the amount banks have on reserve, or by a process called Quantitative Easing (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The chapter's argument about replacement refers to this kind of institution and to the clearing operations that accompany it.

The central bank works by discretion, whereas Bitcoin works by rule. A central bank decides, within its legal mandate, how much money to create, while in Bitcoin the amount created in each block is a function of the block height, written into software that every full node enforces (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The Bitcoin Wiki states the contrast: in a fully decentralized monetary system there is no central authority that regulates the monetary base, and any currency that is generated by a malicious user who does not follow the rules will be rejected by the network (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

To say that Bitcoin replaces the central bank is a claim about the function of issuing money, and the chapter does not claim that Bitcoin provides every other service of the institutions it names. The difference between a policy that people can change and a rule that the software enforces is the point of the comparison, and whether the rule is better is a question of economics that this textbook leaves open. The course asks the student to state the difference accurately and to avoid slogans.

nodes.example: a bank that issues the national currency
nodes.definition: A central bank is the institution that controls the creation of a national currency; Bitcoin has none, and its issuance is set by rules.

nodes.label: Clearing house
nodes.body: A clearing house is a central institution through which payments are recorded and settled. The chapter describes the role when it discusses the digital money that existed before Bitcoin: early digital currencies used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions at regular intervals, just like a traditional banking system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word clearing itself denotes the process by which a payment becomes final; the chapter states that in traditional financial terms the inclusion of a transaction in a block is known as clearing.

paras.text: A clearing house is a central institution through which payments are recorded and settled. The chapter describes the role when it discusses the digital money that existed before Bitcoin: early digital currencies used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions at regular intervals, just like a traditional banking system (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word clearing itself denotes the process by which a payment becomes final; the chapter states that in traditional financial terms the inclusion of a transaction in a block is known as clearing.

The clearing house solves a real problem. Someone has to decide which of two conflicting payments counts, and a central party with a global view of the money in circulation can decide it. The same page of the chapter says that conventional money is also often stored and transmitted digitally and that the counterfeiting and double-spend issues are handled by clearing all electronic transactions through central authorities that have a global view of the currency in circulation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost of the solution is that the whole system depends on one operator.

Clearing houses are met in banking, card payments and securities trading. The whitepaper makes the same point about its predecessor, the trusted mint: the fate of the entire money system depends on the company running the mint, with every transaction having to go through them, just like a bank (Nakamoto, 2008). The early digital currencies of the chapter's sidebar were easy to attack because they had exactly such a central point.

The clearing house keeps one authoritative list of who owns what and processes payments against it. Because it sees all payments in order, it can reject a payment that spends money which is already spent. Bitcoin keeps the same list but distributes the work: every full node holds the list of transactions, and the confirmation of a payment in a block takes the place of the clearing operation. The section on confirmations explains how the network reaches that result without a central party (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Removing the clearing house does not remove the need for clearing; it moves the function into the network. The chapter makes this point when it says that mining decentralizes the clearing function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the clearing in Bitcoin is not instantaneous: the chapter says that a transaction is confirmed when it is included in a block, which happens every 10 minutes on average, and until then it is shown as unconfirmed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a central clearinghouse settling all transactions
nodes.definition: A clearing house is a central party that records and settles transactions; traditional digital money relied on one, and the term clearing means the confirmation of a payment.

nodes.label: Central bank replacement
nodes.body: The replacement of the central bank is the chapter's claim about what mining achieves for the system as a whole. In the words of the chapter, Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two functions are named: issuing the currency and clearing transactions, and mining performs both at once.

paras.text: The replacement of the central bank is the chapter's claim about what mining achieves for the system as a whole. In the words of the chapter, Bitcoin mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two functions are named: issuing the currency and clearing transactions, and mining performs both at once.

The claim explains why Bitcoin needs mining at all. A network of equal participants has no leader who could decide which transactions come first or who could issue new money, so the work of the miner is the substitute for that leader. The reward of a block creates the currency, and the inclusion of transactions in blocks clears them. The incentive for the miner, new bitcoins and fees, pays for the work that keeps the record secure, as the whitepaper explains (Nakamoto, 2008).

The idea is the thread that connects the early sections of the chapter, where mining is introduced, with the later ones on confirmations and clearing. The whitepaper describes the same design from the inside: the network timestamps transactions by hashing them into an ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work, and the first transaction of a block starts a new coin owned by its creator (Nakamoto, 2008). Readers meet the claim again in discussions of whether Bitcoin is money.

The two functions are separate in the protocol. Issuance happens through the subsidy, which the rules allow the miner of each block to claim and which halves on a schedule. Clearing happens through the block, which orders the transactions it contains and so decides which of two conflicting payments comes first. The security of both rests on proof of work, because rewriting an earlier block would require repeating its work and that of all the later blocks.

The word replace should be read narrowly. The mechanism replaces the need for a central issuer and a central clearing operator, which are the two functions that the chapter names. It does not make the system free of intermediaries in practice, because the chapter itself describes users who hold their funds with custodians, exchanges and web services, and these are ordinary companies with the usual risks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: Mining decentralizes the currency-issuance and clearing functions of a central bank and replaces the need for any central bank.

nodes.label: Deflation
nodes.body: Deflation is an increase in the real value of the monetary unit, reflected in a decrease in the general price level of goods and services (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The chapter calls the Bitcoin currency deflationary because of its diminishing rate of issuance: the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, and over the long term the supply grows ever more slowly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The statement is made as a property of the supply schedule, not as a prediction of prices.

paras.text: Deflation is an increase in the real value of the monetary unit, reflected in a decrease in the general price level of goods and services (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The chapter calls the Bitcoin currency deflationary because of its diminishing rate of issuance: the protocol periodically decreases the number of new bitcoins that are created, and over the long term the supply grows ever more slowly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The statement is made as a property of the supply schedule, not as a prediction of prices.

The concept matters because it is one of the first things that economists say about Bitcoin, and it follows directly from the rules of the previous section. If the money supply grows by a shrinking amount while demand for the money does not shrink, each unit tends to buy more over time. The chapter adds a related remark, that nobody can force you to accept any bitcoins that were created beyond the expected issuance rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Both statements come from the same schedule.

The schedule can be read from the rules of Bitcoin Core. The subsidy is computed by shifting 50 bitcoin right by the number of halvings, and 33 halvings reduce the subsidy to zero, because 50 * 10**8 satoshis shifted right 33 places is 0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The 33 eras of 210,000 blocks make 6,930,000 blocks, the last block with a non-zero subsidy being the one just before that height. The Bitcoin Wiki discusses the same ending under the heading of what happens when all the bitcoins are mined (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).

The first block of the network was created on 2009-01-03 at 18:15:05 UTC, according to the time stamp 1231006505 in the block data (Blockstream, 2026). If blocks were produced exactly every 10 minutes, the height 6,930,000 would be reached after 6,930,000 * 600 seconds, and the example program adds that number of seconds to the time of the first block and prints the date 2140-10-08. The date is an estimate that rests on the assumption of a perfect 10-minute pace, and the actual pace depends on the difficulty adjustment.

Deflationary does not mean that the price of bitcoin must rise, and the chapter does not say so; it describes the issuance. The effect on prices is a question of economics that depends on many factors besides the supply schedule. Finally, the end of the subsidy does not end mining: the miner's income then consists of fees, which is why the whitepaper observes that the incentive can transition entirely to transaction fees and be completely inflation free (Nakamoto, 2008).

nodes.example: the date when the subsidy reaches zero
nodes.definition: Because issuance diminishes and ends, the currency is deflationary over the long term; the last non-zero subsidy falls in the year 2140 at the target pace.

nodes.label: Network
nodes.body: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader. The chapter describes Bitcoin as a distributed, peer-to-peer system in which there is no central server or point of control, and as a protocol, a peer-to-peer network, and a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch contains the ideas of consensus, which is the agreement, and of history, which tells how the system came to exist.

paras.text: The Network branch is about the community of computers that runs Bitcoin and the way it agrees on a single history without a leader. The chapter describes Bitcoin as a distributed, peer-to-peer system in which there is no central server or point of control, and as a protocol, a peer-to-peer network, and a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch contains the ideas of consensus, which is the agreement, and of history, which tells how the system came to exist.

A money system that is held together by many independent computers must solve a hard problem: those computers have to agree on which payments happened, even though they receive messages in different orders and some of them may be dishonest. The solution is the main technical achievement of Bitcoin, and the chapter presents it as a breakthrough in distributed computing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Without an understanding of the agreement mechanism, the rest of the course reads as a list of unrelated parts.

The network appears whenever the chapter speaks about transactions travelling from Joe's wallet to Alice's wallet, about miners, and about the nodes that validate. The historical part appears in the section named History of Bitcoin, which cites the 2008 paper, the start of the network in 2009, and the withdrawal of its inventor from the public in 2011 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has three sections. The Consensus section explains proof of work, the double-spend problem it solves, the mining by which blocks are produced, the adjustment of difficulty that keeps the pace constant, and the problem in distributed computing that Bitcoin's design answers. The History section tells who proposed the system and what it built on. The Standards section explains the two social mechanisms through which the system is documented and governed: the numbered improvement proposals and open source software.

It is easy to imagine the network as a company with servers, and the chapter warns against that picture; there is no central server. It is equally easy to imagine consensus as a vote of people, whereas the agreement is reached by software that checks the same rules and follows the chain with the most work. The branch should be read with both corrections in mind.

nodes.label: Consensus
nodes.body: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions. The chapter says that the proof-of-work algorithm is a mechanism for reaching global decentralized consensus on the valid blockchain, and that a key innovation was to use a distributed computation system to conduct a global lottery every 10 minutes on average, allowing the decentralized network to arrive at consensus about the state of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Consensus is the state in which the participants of the network agree on the same record of transactions. The chapter says that the proof-of-work algorithm is a mechanism for reaching global decentralized consensus on the valid blockchain, and that a key innovation was to use a distributed computation system to conduct a global lottery every 10 minutes on average, allowing the decentralized network to arrive at consensus about the state of transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Consensus is what turns a crowd of computers into a ledger. Without it, two participants could hold different histories and each could claim that the other's payments never happened. The consensus mechanism is also what protects against the double-spend, the main threat to any digital money, so the concepts of this section explain the security of the entire system.

The section contains five concepts. Proof of work is the costly computation that makes a block hard to produce and easy to check. The double-spend is the attack that the whole scheme is designed to prevent. Mining is the activity of performing the work, difficulty adjustment keeps the pace at one block in 10 minutes, and the Byzantine Generals' Problem is the classical problem in distributed computing that the design solves. Concepts of the Foundations branch, such as the hash function, are used here and explained there.

nodes.label: Proof of work
nodes.body: Proof of work is a way of showing that a certain amount of computation has been spent, in a form that anyone can check cheaply. In Bitcoin it is the method by which the network decides which block comes next. The whitepaper describes it as scanning for a value that, when hashed with a function such as SHA-256, gives a hash that begins with a number of zero bits; the average work required is exponential in the number of zero bits and can be verified by executing a single hash (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter calls the mechanism the proof-of-work algorithm and says that it conducts a global lottery every 10 minutes on average (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Proof of work is a way of showing that a certain amount of computation has been spent, in a form that anyone can check cheaply. In Bitcoin it is the method by which the network decides which block comes next. The whitepaper describes it as scanning for a value that, when hashed with a function such as SHA-256, gives a hash that begins with a number of zero bits; the average work required is exponential in the number of zero bits and can be verified by executing a single hash (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter calls the mechanism the proof-of-work algorithm and says that it conducts a global lottery every 10 minutes on average (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The purpose of the work is to make agreement possible without trust. If producing a block were free, anyone could produce as many as they liked and the network could not choose between them. By making each block costly, proof of work turns the choice into a measurable quantity: the whitepaper observes that proof of work is essentially one-CPU-one-vote, and that the majority decision is represented by the longest chain, the one with the greatest proof-of-work effort invested in it (Nakamoto, 2008). This also solves the problem that a vote by network address could be subverted by anyone able to allocate many addresses.

The idea was not new when Bitcoin appeared. The chapter says that Nakamoto combined several prior inventions such as digital signatures and Hashcash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and Back's paper describes Hashcash as a mechanism, proposed in 1997, to throttle systematic abuse of un-metered internet resources such as email (Back, 2002). In Bitcoin the work is done by the miners, for every block, and checked by every node that receives the block. The first block of the network has a hash with ten leading zeros in hexadecimal notation, 000000000019d668, according to the Bitcoin Core source (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The example is a miniature of the real process. The program tries the numbers 0, 1, 2 and so on, forms the text SEN0401- followed by the number, computes the SHA-256 hash of that text, and stops at the first number whose hash in hexadecimal notation starts with four zeros. The first such number is 15083, found after 15084 attempts, and the hash of the text SEN0401-15083 starts with 0000a1fa. Each hexadecimal digit has 16 possible values, so a prefix of four zeros is expected once in 16 to the fourth power, that is 65536, attempts. Checking the claim, by contrast, takes a single hash computation.

Proof of work does not prove that the transactions in a block are valid; validity is checked separately by every node, and a block with an invalid transaction is rejected however much work was spent on it. The work is also not useful computation in itself: its value lies in its cost. A further misconception is that the work is a puzzle that can be solved by cleverness; since a hash function behaves unpredictably, the only method is to try values, and the winner is determined by chance in proportion to the computing power used.

nodes.example: a toy search for a hash starting with 0000
nodes.definition: Proof of work makes adding a block costly and easy to check; a toy version searches for a number whose SHA-256 hash starts with zeros.

nodes.label: Double-spend
nodes.body: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Physical money addresses the problem easily, because the same paper note cannot be in two places at once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); digital money cannot rely on that physical fact.

paras.text: The double-spend is the act of spending the same unit of digital money more than once. The chapter lists it as the second of three basic questions for anyone accepting digital money: can I trust that the digital money can only be spent once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Physical money addresses the problem easily, because the same paper note cannot be in two places at once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); digital money cannot rely on that physical fact.

A digital currency that cannot prevent double-spending is worthless, since the recipient could never be sure that the money received had not already been paid to someone else. Before Bitcoin the problem was handled by clearing every transaction through a central clearinghouse; the chapter calls this a weakness because the central party becomes a single point of attack, and it says that Nakamoto's proof of work elegantly solves the problem without it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The whitepaper begins with exactly this problem. Its abstract notes that digital signatures provide part of the solution, but that the main benefits are lost if a trusted third party is still required to prevent double-spending (Nakamoto, 2008). In practice a double-spend is attempted when a payer sends one transaction to a merchant and a conflicting one to the network, hoping that the second wins. The merchant protects himself by waiting for confirmations.

The defence is a public, ordered record. The whitepaper explains that the only way to confirm the absence of a transaction is to be aware of all transactions, and that without a trusted party the transactions must be publicly announced, and the participants need a system to agree on a single history of the order in which they were received; the earliest transaction is the one that counts (Nakamoto, 2008). The example is a toy ledger in which a set remembers the spent coins: the first spend of coin7 is accepted, giving True, and the second is rejected, giving False. Bitcoin does the same at network scale, with blocks as the record.

A double-spend is not made impossible by cryptography alone; a digital signature proves who authorised a payment and does not show that the payment is the only one. The protection is a consequence of consensus and gets stronger with each confirmation, so a transaction that is not yet confirmed can still be replaced by a conflicting one. The toy ledger above also shows only the principle, because a real network has no single machine that keeps the set.

nodes.definition: The double-spend problem is the possibility of spending one unit of digital money twice; Bitcoin's consensus prevents it without a central clearinghouse.
