nodes.label: Mining
nodes.body: Mining is the process by which new blocks are produced and new bitcoins are created. The chapter describes it as repeatedly performing a computational task that references a list of recent Bitcoin transactions, and it says that any participant in the network may operate as a miner, using their computing devices to help secure transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A miner is therefore a participant that competes to find the next block.

paras.text: Mining is the process by which new blocks are produced and new bitcoins are created. The chapter describes it as repeatedly performing a computational task that references a list of recent Bitcoin transactions, and it says that any participant in the network may operate as a miner, using their computing devices to help secure transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A miner is therefore a participant that competes to find the next block.

Mining fulfils two purposes that a central bank would otherwise fulfil. It creates the currency, because the miner who finds a block is rewarded with brand new bitcoins and the fees paid by recent transactions, and it secures the record, because the work spent on a block makes the block costly to rewrite. The chapter says that every 10 minutes, on average, one miner can add security to past transactions, and that mining decentralizes the issuance and clearing functions of a central bank (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Mining may be done by a participant alone or together with others in a pool, a form that the glossary of the book calls pooled mining and describes as multiple generating clients contributing to the generation of a block and splitting the reward according to the contributed processing power (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper compares the effort with gold mining, in which resources are expended to add gold to circulation, and names CPU time and electricity as what is expended in Bitcoin (Nakamoto, 2008).

The cycle follows the steps of the whitepaper. Transactions are broadcast to the nodes, each miner collects new transactions into a block, works on finding a difficult proof of work for the block, and when it succeeds it broadcasts the block; the other nodes accept it only if all transactions in it are valid and not already spent, and they signal acceptance by working on the next block that builds on it (Nakamoto, 2008). At the target pace of one block in 10 minutes, a day of 24 * 60 minutes yields 144 blocks on average, the result of the example expression.

The word mining suggests that coins are dug out of the ground one by one. What the miner actually finds is a valid block, and the new coins are a payment attached to it. Mining is also not a guaranteed income: because the search is a lottery, a single machine may work for a very long time without finding a block, which is the reason for pools. Finally, the share of the reward that comes from new coins falls with each halving, and the miners' revenue then depends increasingly on fees.

nodes.definition: Mining is the repeated computation, referring to a list of recent transactions, by which a participant tries to add a block and earn the reward.

nodes.label: Difficulty adjustment
nodes.body: The difficulty adjustment is the rule that keeps the pace of the network constant. The chapter says that the difficulty of the computational task that miners must perform is adjusted dynamically so that, on average, someone succeeds every 10 minutes regardless of how many miners, and how much processing, are competing at any moment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The difficulty is a measure of how hard it is to find a valid block; a higher difficulty requires more attempts.

paras.text: The difficulty adjustment is the rule that keeps the pace of the network constant. The chapter says that the difficulty of the computational task that miners must perform is adjusted dynamically so that, on average, someone succeeds every 10 minutes regardless of how many miners, and how much processing, are competing at any moment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The difficulty is a measure of how hard it is to find a valid block; a higher difficulty requires more attempts.

Without an adjustment, the pace of blocks would depend on the number of machines. If many new machines joined, blocks would arrive in seconds and the schedule of the supply would run ahead of its calendar; if many machines left, the network would slow to a crawl. The whitepaper gives the same reason: to compensate for increasing hardware speed and varying interest in running nodes over time, the difficulty is determined by a moving average targeting an average number of blocks per hour (Nakamoto, 2008).

The rule is part of the consensus code of Bitcoin Core. The parameters of the main network set the target spacing to 10 * 60 seconds and the target timespan to 14 * 24 * 60 * 60 seconds, two weeks, and the number of blocks between adjustments is their quotient, 2016 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The glossary of the book describes the same recalculation as taking place once every 2,016 blocks and considering the hashing power of the previous 2,016 blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

At the end of every period of 2016 blocks, the nodes compare the time that the period actually took with the intended two weeks and scale the target accordingly: the new target is the old target multiplied by the actual timespan and divided by the intended timespan. If the period took only one week, the new target is half the old one; the target is the number below which a block's hash must lie, so a smaller target means that finding a valid block requires more attempts and becomes twice as hard (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core limits the step: an actual timespan shorter than a quarter, or longer than four times, the intended one is replaced by that limit (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A real example is the difference between the hash of the first block, which begins with 10 zeros, and that of block 840000, which begins with 19 zeros (Blockstream, 2026).

The adjustment lags: the network reacts only after a period of 2016 blocks, so in the short run the pace can differ much from 10 minutes. It also does not control the price or the supply directly; it controls the pace. The figure of 10 minutes is a target and an average, and the time to the next block follows a random distribution, so that a block can come seconds or an hour after the previous one.

nodes.example: 2016 blocks in two weeks at 10 minutes each
nodes.definition: The difficulty of the work is adjusted every 2016 blocks so that, on average, one block is found every 10 minutes whatever the total computing power.

nodes.label: Byzantine Generals' Problem
nodes.body: The Byzantine Generals' Problem is a classical problem in distributed computing. The chapter describes it briefly as the problem of trying to get multiple participants without a leader to agree on a course of action by exchanging information over an unreliable and potentially compromised network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The original paper expresses the situation as a group of generals of the Byzantine army camped around an enemy city who can communicate only by messenger and must agree upon a common battle plan, although one or more of them may be traitors who will try to confuse the others (Lamport et al., 1982).

paras.text: The Byzantine Generals' Problem is a classical problem in distributed computing. The chapter describes it briefly as the problem of trying to get multiple participants without a leader to agree on a course of action by exchanging information over an unreliable and potentially compromised network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The original paper expresses the situation as a group of generals of the Byzantine army camped around an enemy city who can communicate only by messenger and must agree upon a common battle plan, although one or more of them may be traitors who will try to confuse the others (Lamport et al., 1982).

The problem is the abstract form of the challenge that a money network faces. The participants are the computers, the course of action is the next block, and the traitors are dishonest participants who want to double-spend. The chapter calls Satoshi Nakamoto's invention a practical and novel solution to this problem and says that its use of proof of work to achieve consensus without a central trusted authority represents a breakthrough in distributed computing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The problem was stated in 1982 by Lamport, Shostak and Pease, who wrote that reliable computer systems must handle malfunctioning components that give conflicting information to different parts of the system (Lamport et al., 1982). The whitepaper does not use the name, but its abstract describes the answer in the same terms: the network itself requires minimal structure, messages are broadcast on a best effort basis, and nodes can leave and rejoin the network at will, accepting the longest proof-of-work chain as proof of what happened while they were gone (Nakamoto, 2008).

The 1982 paper proves that with oral messages the problem is solvable if and only if more than two-thirds of the generals are loyal, and that with unforgeable written messages it is solvable for any number of traitors (Lamport et al., 1982). Bitcoin's participants are not a fixed, known set of generals, so proof of work changes the counting rule: the weight of a participant is not a name or an address but the computational work it can show. The whitepaper states that if a majority of computing power is controlled by honest nodes, the honest chain will grow the fastest and outpace any competing chains, and an attacker would have to redo the work of the block and of all blocks after it (Nakamoto, 2008).

The solution is probabilistic, not absolute. A node can never be mathematically certain that a block is final; the chance that it will be reversed falls with every block added after it, which is the reason for waiting for confirmations. And the guarantee depends on an assumption, namely that honest participants control the majority of the computing power; the story of the generals stays a useful reminder that this assumption is what the security rests on.

nodes.example: generals agreeing to attack by messenger
nodes.definition: The Byzantine Generals' Problem asks how participants without a leader can agree on a course of action over an unreliable network; Bitcoin's proof of work is a practical solution.

nodes.label: History
nodes.body: The History section tells where Bitcoin came from. The chapter describes the system as first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper under the alias Satoshi Nakamoto, as started in 2009 on a reference implementation, and as left in April 2011 to a group of volunteers when its inventor withdrew from the public (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also contains the sidebar on digital currencies before Bitcoin and the origin of proof of work in Hashcash.

paras.text: The History section tells where Bitcoin came from. The chapter describes the system as first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper under the alias Satoshi Nakamoto, as started in 2009 on a reference implementation, and as left in April 2011 to a group of volunteers when its inventor withdrew from the public (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also contains the sidebar on digital currencies before Bitcoin and the origin of proof of work in Hashcash.

History explains why the design looks as it does. Bitcoin was not invented from nothing: it combined prior inventions such as digital signatures and Hashcash, and it answered the failure of earlier centralized digital currencies, which were targeted by governments and attacked by hackers. A student who knows the history can distinguish what was new in Bitcoin from what was inherited.

The five concepts of the section run from the past to the present. Prior digital currencies and Hashcash describe what existed before. The whitepaper and its author describe the proposal. The reference implementation describes the first software, which is still developed and maintained today. Taken together, they show the system as a chain of dated steps that can be checked against the sources.

nodes.label: Whitepaper
nodes.body: The whitepaper is the paper in which Bitcoin was first described. The chapter says that Bitcoin was first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A whitepaper, in general, is a document that presents a technical proposal; in Bitcoin's case, the paper is nine pages long and is reprinted as an appendix of the book.

paras.text: The whitepaper is the paper in which Bitcoin was first described. The chapter says that Bitcoin was first described in 2008 with the publication of a paper titled Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A whitepaper, in general, is a document that presents a technical proposal; in Bitcoin's case, the paper is nine pages long and is reprinted as an appendix of the book.

The paper matters because it states the design in the author's own words, and because every later description of Bitcoin is an interpretation of it. Its abstract proposes a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash that would allow online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution, and it proposes a solution to the double-spending problem using a peer-to-peer network (Nakamoto, 2008).

The paper is cited throughout the course. Its sections are named Transactions, Timestamp Server, Proof-of-Work, Network, Incentive, Reclaiming Disk Space, Simplified Payment Verification, Combining and Splitting Value, Privacy, and Calculations (Nakamoto, 2008), and later chapters of the book take up each of them. It also gives the first definition of the electronic coin: a chain of digital signatures, in which each owner transfers the coin to the next by signing a hash of the previous transaction and the public key of the next owner.

The title already states the proposal: a system for electronic cash in which the parties deal with each other directly, as peers. The paper's argument proceeds in order. It states that commerce on the internet relies on trusted third parties, argues that what is needed is an electronic payment system based on cryptographic proof instead of trust, and then builds the solution from the transaction, the timestamp server, the proof of work and the network (Nakamoto, 2008).

The whitepaper is not a specification. It leaves out details that the software had to settle, and the system has changed since 2008 in ways that the paper does not describe. A second observation concerns vocabulary: the saved text of the paper does not contain the word blockchain at all, and it speaks of a chain of blocks and of the longest proof-of-work chain (Nakamoto, 2008). The author's identity does not affect the text, which can be checked on its own merits.

nodes.example: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System
nodes.definition: The 2008 paper by Satoshi Nakamoto that first described Bitcoin as a purely peer-to-peer version of electronic cash.

nodes.label: Reference implementation
nodes.body: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the standard against which other programs are compared. For Bitcoin it is the software that implements the protocol and that includes a wallet, known as Bitcoin Core, which the chapter says is derived from the original implementation written by Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network started in 2009, based on a reference implementation published by Nakamoto and since revised by many other programmers.

paras.text: A reference implementation is a program that serves as the standard against which other programs are compared. For Bitcoin it is the software that implements the protocol and that includes a wallet, known as Bitcoin Core, which the chapter says is derived from the original implementation written by Satoshi Nakamoto (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network started in 2009, based on a reference implementation published by Nakamoto and since revised by many other programmers.

Bitcoin has no written specification that is complete in itself, so the behaviour of the reference implementation has in practice defined what is valid. This is why other programs that speak the protocol are tested against it. The chapter compares the situation with the web: a Bitcoin wallet is the most common user interface of the system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol HTTP, and many brands exist for both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin Core's source code can be read, and its consensus rules are in files such as the one that computes the block subsidy and the one that adjusts the difficulty. The second file still carries a copyright line for 2009 to 2010 in the name of Satoshi Nakamoto, followed by one for the Bitcoin Core developers (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Chapter 3 of the book, titled Bitcoin Core: The Reference Implementation, is devoted to it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The copyright line in the file pow.cpp, which reads Copyright (c) 2009-2010 Satoshi Nakamoto, is evidence that the present code descends from the code that Nakamoto published. In the chapter's terms the program can act as a full node, which validates the entire history of transactions and can serve data to other programs, and it includes a wallet for the user's keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reference implementation is a practical standard, and not a guarantee of correctness. The phrase means that the program is the one against which the behaviour of others is judged, not that it is the only program that could exist. A student should therefore distinguish the protocol, which the chapter describes as a peer-to-peer network, from Bitcoin Core, which is one program that speaks it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The software that Nakamoto published in 2009 and many programmers have revised since; Bitcoin Core is its descendant and includes a wallet.

nodes.label: Satoshi Nakamoto
nodes.body: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation. The glossary of the book adds that they devised the first blockchain database, that they were the first to solve the double-spending problem for digital currency, and that their real identity remains unknown (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter states that the whitepaper was written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto.

paras.text: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name used by the person or people who designed Bitcoin and created its original reference implementation. The glossary of the book adds that they devised the first blockchain database, that they were the first to solve the double-spending problem for digital currency, and that their real identity remains unknown (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter states that the whitepaper was written under the alias of Satoshi Nakamoto.

The question of the author matters less for a technical course than it might seem, and the chapter explains why. Satoshi Nakamoto withdrew from the public in April 2011, leaving the responsibility of developing the code and network to a thriving group of volunteers, and neither Nakamoto nor anyone else exerts individual control over the Bitcoin system, which operates on fully transparent mathematical principles, open source code, and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A system without an owner does not need a known founder.

The name appears in the title page of the whitepaper, in the copyright line of old source files, and in the name of the satoshi unit. The author of the paper gave an email address in the paper, satoshin@gmx.com, and the site bitcoin.org (Nakamoto, 2008), but nothing in the text identifies a person.

What can be said from the sources is limited. The paper dates from 2008, the first block of the network is stamped 2009-01-03, the code was published in 2009, and the public involvement ended in April 2011 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter combines these facts to describe the author as a person or group who built the first version and then left. All technical claims in this course are checked against the paper and the code and not against assumptions about the author.

Two pitfalls are common. The first is to treat claims about the identity as facts; the book says the identity is unknown, and so does this text. The second is to confuse the author with the unit: Satoshi Nakamoto is a person or group, while the satoshi, the unit of one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin, is only named after the author. A student should also avoid appeals to the authority of the author, since the rules of Bitcoin are those enforced by the software that participants run today.

nodes.definition: Satoshi Nakamoto is the alias of the person or people who designed Bitcoin; their identity is unknown and they withdrew from the public in April 2011.

nodes.label: Hashcash
nodes.body: Hashcash is a proof-of-work system proposed by Adam Back. His paper states that Hashcash was originally proposed as a mechanism to throttle systematic abuse of un-metered internet resources such as email and anonymous remailers in May 1997, and that its cost-function computes a token which can be used as a proof-of-work (Back, 2002). The chapter lists Hashcash, together with digital signatures, among the prior inventions that Nakamoto combined (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Hashcash is a proof-of-work system proposed by Adam Back. His paper states that Hashcash was originally proposed as a mechanism to throttle systematic abuse of un-metered internet resources such as email and anonymous remailers in May 1997, and that its cost-function computes a token which can be used as a proof-of-work (Back, 2002). The chapter lists Hashcash, together with digital signatures, among the prior inventions that Nakamoto combined (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Hashcash showed that a cost in computation could replace a cost in money or an identity check. The paper reasons that if there is a cost associated with sending each email, this may be sufficient to limit the scale of email abuse perpetrated by spammers (Back, 2002). Back's paper requires that a cost-function should be efficiently verifiable but parameterisably expensive to compute (Back, 2002), and the same two properties are what Bitcoin needed: expensive to produce, cheap to check.

The whitepaper cites Hashcash by name when it introduces its proof of work: to implement a distributed timestamp server on a peer-to-peer basis, it uses a proof-of-work system similar to Adam Back's Hashcash (Nakamoto, 2008). The concept is found today in anti-abuse systems and in the mining of many currencies. The chapter's sidebar on digital currencies before Bitcoin explains the setting in which such ideas were being tried.

Back's paper defines the Hashcash cost-function as finding partial hash collisions on the all-zero bit string, and notes that the fastest algorithm for computing partial collisions is brute force; the client can safely choose its own random challenge, and anyone can efficiently verify a published token (Back, 2002). In other words, the sender tries values until the hash of the combination begins with a required number of zero bits, and the receiver checks the claim with a single hash. In the example, the hash of the text SEN0401-15083 is written as 256 bits and its first 1 bit is at position 16, so the hash begins with 16 zero bits, which is exactly what four zero hexadecimal digits mean. Each additional zero bit doubles the expected number of attempts.

Hashcash on its own does not solve double-spending: it limits the rate at which tokens can be produced, and the paper itself says that the server needs to keep a double spending database of spent tokens, to detect and reject attempts to spend the same token again (Back, 2002). Bitcoin removes the server: the whitepaper adds a chain of blocks, in which each block includes the hash of the previous block, and a rule that the longest chain, the one with the most work, counts as correct (Nakamoto, 2008). A second caution is that the cost of the work depends on hardware, which is why Bitcoin adjusts its difficulty.
