nodes.definition: Hashcash is a proof-of-work scheme proposed by Adam Back in 1997 to throttle abuse of un-metered resources such as email; Bitcoin's proof of work descends from it.

nodes.label: Digital currencies before Bitcoin
nodes.body: Digital currencies before Bitcoin were the early attempts, starting in the late 1980s, to use cryptography to build digital money. The chapter's sidebar says that when cryptography started becoming more broadly available and understood in the late 1980s, many researchers began trying to use it to build digital currencies, and that these early projects issued digital money, usually backed by a national currency or a precious metal such as gold (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Digital currencies before Bitcoin were the early attempts, starting in the late 1980s, to use cryptography to build digital money. The chapter's sidebar says that when cryptography started becoming more broadly available and understood in the late 1980s, many researchers began trying to use it to build digital currencies, and that these early projects issued digital money, usually backed by a national currency or a precious metal such as gold (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The failures of these projects define the problem that Bitcoin solved. The chapter reports that although the earlier currencies worked, they were centralized and, as a result, were easy to attack by governments and hackers; they used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions at regular intervals, and in most cases they were targeted by worried governments and eventually litigated out of existence, while some failed in spectacular crashes when the parent company liquidated abruptly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The sidebar frames three questions that anyone accepting digital money must answer: whether the money is authentic and not counterfeit, whether it can only be spent once, and whether no one else can claim that it belongs to them and not to the holder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Issuers of paper money fight counterfeiting with increasingly sophisticated paper and printing technology, which digital money cannot use, so cryptography takes its place.

Cryptography supplies the answer to authenticity: cryptographic digital signatures enable a user to sign a digital asset or transaction, proving the ownership of that asset, and with the appropriate architecture the same signatures can be used to address the double-spend issue (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The architecture is what the earlier projects got wrong. They placed it in a central clearinghouse, whereas Bitcoin places it in a decentralized network.

The lesson of the sidebar is not that digital money is impossible without a network of equals, but that a central operator can be a single point of attack or of failure. The chapter's conclusion is that to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, a decentralized digital currency was needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should read that as a claim about design robustness, not as a statement of what is legal in any country.

nodes.definition: Digital currencies before Bitcoin used cryptography but were centralized and therefore easy to attack, which is the problem Bitcoin was designed to avoid.

nodes.label: Standards and openness
nodes.body: The Standards section collects the two social mechanisms through which Bitcoin is documented and developed: the numbered improvement proposals through which changes are discussed, and the open source licence under which the software is shared. Both appear in the chapter indirectly, in the references to the recovery code standard and to the open source software that runs the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Standards section collects the two social mechanisms through which Bitcoin is documented and developed: the numbered improvement proposals through which changes are discussed, and the open source licence under which the software is shared. Both appear in the chapter indirectly, in the references to the recovery code standard and to the open source software that runs the network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A system without an owner needs a way to evolve. Proposals must be written down, discussed, and accepted or rejected in public, and the code must be available to anyone who wants to check or reuse it. These two practices are what allow a community of volunteers, rather than a company, to maintain a system that holds real value.

The first concept of the section is the Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, the document in which a change or a convention is specified. The second one is open source software, the legal and practical form in which Bitcoin Core and most wallets are published. Together they explain how a standard such as the one for recovery codes, discussed in the Wallet branch, can be shared by programs from different authors.

nodes.label: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP)
nodes.body: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a numbered document in which a member of the community proposes a change to Bitcoin or describes a convention that programs should follow. The glossary of the book defines BIPs as a set of proposals that members of the Bitcoin community have submitted to improve Bitcoin, and gives BIP21, a proposal to improve the bitcoin uniform resource identifier scheme, as an example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal, abbreviated BIP, is a numbered document in which a member of the community proposes a change to Bitcoin or describes a convention that programs should follow. The glossary of the book defines BIPs as a set of proposals that members of the Bitcoin community have submitted to improve Bitcoin, and gives BIP21, a proposal to improve the bitcoin uniform resource identifier scheme, as an example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

BIPs give a decentralized project a public memory and a procedure. Every proposal has a number, an author, a status such as Deployed, and a type such as Specification, and it is available for anyone to read; the header of BIP 39 shows these fields (Palatinus et al., 2013). Because wallets of different authors can follow the same document, a user can move from one program to another, which is only possible when the convention is written down.

The book collects the proposals that matter for Bitcoin Core in an appendix, which lists, for instance, BIP32 on hierarchical deterministic wallets and BIP173 on Bech32 addresses, with the release of Bitcoin Core in which each was implemented (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The recovery codes of this chapter follow BIP 39, titled Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys, which describes the implementation of a mnemonic code or sentence, a group of easy-to-remember words, for the generation of deterministic wallets (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The example takes numbers directly from BIP 39. Its table relates the length of the initial entropy ENT, the length of the checksum CS = ENT / 32, and the number of words MS = (ENT + CS) / 11: an entropy of 128 bits has a checksum of 4 bits and gives 12 words, and an entropy of 256 bits has a checksum of 8 bits and gives 24 words (Palatinus et al., 2013). The program computes the same triples, (128, 4, 12) and (256, 8, 24), and the match with the table shows that the specification can be checked by executing it.

A BIP is a proposal and not a law. Its header records a status, and BIP 39 carries the status Deployed (Palatinus et al., 2013), which says that programs implement it; a proposal without that status gives no one an obligation. The appendix of the book lists which proposals Bitcoin Core implements and since which release, and the lesson is that a change takes effect only when the software that participants run contains it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: A Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP) is a numbered design document that specifies a change or a convention; BIP 39 describes the mnemonic code behind recovery codes.

nodes.label: Open source software
nodes.body: Open source software is software whose source code is available to everyone and whose licence allows it to be used, studied, changed and redistributed. The Open Source Definition states that open source does not just mean access to the source code, and lists criteria that the distribution terms must meet, among them free redistribution, the inclusion of source code, and permission for modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026).

paras.text: Open source software is software whose source code is available to everyone and whose licence allows it to be used, studied, changed and redistributed. The Open Source Definition states that open source does not just mean access to the source code, and lists criteria that the distribution terms must meet, among them free redistribution, the inclusion of source code, and permission for modifications and derived works (Open Source Initiative, 2026).

Openness is part of why a system like Bitcoin can be trusted without a company behind it. The chapter says that the Bitcoin protocol stack is available as open source software and can be run on a wide range of computing devices, including laptops and smartphones, making the technology easily accessible, and that Bitcoin operates based on fully transparent mathematical principles, open source code, and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The source file of the difficulty rule in Bitcoin Core says that it is distributed under the MIT software license (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A licence of this kind is what turns published source code into open source software in the sense of the Open Source Definition (Open Source Initiative, 2026). The chapter states that the protocol stack is available as open source software, and that it runs on laptops and smartphones alike (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Because the code is open, anyone can read the rules that the software enforces, compile their own copy, and check that it matches the published release. A participant does not have to trust a vendor; he can inspect the code or rely on others who do. When a flaw is found, anyone can propose a fix, and the improvement process of the BIPs provides the place to discuss it.

Open source does not mean that the code has been reviewed by everyone, and it does not mean that anyone can change the rules of the network. A change in the code reaches the network only if enough participants choose to run it. The chapter stresses that wallets vary in quality, performance, security, privacy and reliability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), so a student should not assume that every program that handles bitcoin is of equal quality merely because the protocol is open.

nodes.example: Bitcoin Core published under a licence
nodes.definition: Open source software is distributed with its source code under terms that allow free redistribution, modification and derived works.

nodes.label: W3C standard
nodes.body: The World Wide Web Consortium, abbreviated W3C, is an international public-interest non-profit organisation where member organisations, a full-time staff and the public work together to develop web standards (World Wide Web Consortium, 2026). It was founded by Tim Berners-Lee in 1994. A finished standard of the consortium is called a Recommendation.

paras.text: The World Wide Web Consortium, abbreviated W3C, is an international public-interest non-profit organisation where member organisations, a full-time staff and the public work together to develop web standards (World Wide Web Consortium, 2026). It was founded by Tim Berners-Lee in 1994. A finished standard of the consortium is called a Recommendation.

Open standards are what let software from different makers work together on the web, and W3C is where many of them are agreed. This chapter uses two of its Recommendations as a bridge to identity: the Decentralized Identifiers v1.0 of 19 July 2022 and the Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0 of 15 May 2025 (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025). Both express, in a standard form, the idea that control belongs to whoever holds the keys.

Besides identity, the consortium is known for the standards behind web pages and for those behind the semantic web, which is the theme of this course, so a student of SEN0401 meets its documents in both halves of the syllabus. Its Recommendations are public documents that anyone may read without a fee or a licence, which is why this chapter can cite them in the same way that it cites a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal. The two that are cited here, the Decentralized Identifiers and the Verifiable Credentials Data Model, each publish a dated version at a fixed address: the identifier document is the Recommendation of 19 July 2022 and the credentials document the Recommendation of 15 May 2025 (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025). The consortium's own pages state its purpose in one line, that its mission is to make the web work for everyone, and record that Tim Berners-Lee founded it in 1994 to ensure the long-term growth of the web (World Wide Web Consortium, 2026).

A standard moves through drafts and review by the member organisations and by the public before it becomes a Recommendation, and the finished document is the one that implementers are expected to follow. Each document records its status and its date at the top of its first page, and it gives two addresses: one for this particular version, which never changes, and one for the latest published version, which moves on when a new Recommendation appears (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022) (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025). A reader can therefore always say which text he is reading, which matters in a course that quotes it. Programs that implement the standard can then be tested against that fixed text, and two independent implementations that both follow it should be able to work together, which is the practical purpose of the whole process.

A Recommendation is a standard and not a law: it binds only those who choose to implement it, and its authority comes from the number of programs that do so rather than from any power to compel. A document that exists is therefore not evidence that the technology it describes is in wide use, and a student should say that a standard specifies a thing rather than that it establishes it. The Recommendations of this consortium should also be told apart from the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals of the earlier section, which are produced by a different community with its own numbering and its own process, even though both are public, numbered documents that specify how something is to be done.

nodes.definition: The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) is an international organization that develops web standards; its finished standards are called Recommendations.

nodes.label: Wallet
nodes.body: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch collects everything the chapter says about choosing, classifying and protecting a wallet.

paras.text: A wallet is the software through which a person uses Bitcoin. The chapter calls the Bitcoin wallet the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just as a web browser is the most common user interface for the protocol of the web, and the glossary of the book describes it as software that holds your Bitcoin addresses and secret keys and lets you send, receive and store your bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch collects everything the chapter says about choosing, classifying and protecting a wallet.

A wallet is where the abstract rules of the network meet a human being. It decides how much of the work of validation the user does himself, who holds the keys that control the money, and what happens when a phone is lost. The chapter says that wallets vary in quality, performance, security, privacy and reliability, and that choosing a wallet is highly subjective and depends on the use and the user's expertise, so that it would be pointless to recommend a specific brand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Wallets are the most visible applications of the ecosystem and the chapter notes that they are one of the most actively developed ones, with intense competition: a new wallet is probably being developed right now, while several wallets from last year are no longer actively maintained (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every example in the chapter, from Alice's first start-up to Joe's payment, takes place inside a wallet.

The chapter classifies wallets in three ways, and the branch follows them. By platform, there are desktop, mobile, web and hardware wallets. By autonomy, there are full nodes, lightweight clients and third-party API clients. By control, there are noncustodial wallets, where the user holds the keys, and custodial services, where a third party does. A fourth section is about backup, because a user who holds the keys must also be able to restore them.

The three classifications are independent and combine freely. The chapter notes that many wallets fall into a few groups, the three most common being the desktop full node, the mobile lightweight wallet, and the web-based account with a third party, but that the lines between categories are sometimes blurry because software runs on multiple platforms and can interact with the network in different ways (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should therefore describe a wallet along all three dimensions.

nodes.label: Wallet platform
nodes.body: The platform of a wallet is the kind of device and software environment on which it runs. The chapter's section on the types of Bitcoin wallets categorises wallets first by platform and lists the desktop wallet, the mobile wallet, the web wallet and the hardware signing device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The platform determines how convenient the wallet is, how exposed it is to attack, and how much of the user's data is revealed to others.

paras.text: The platform of a wallet is the kind of device and software environment on which it runs. The chapter's section on the types of Bitcoin wallets categorises wallets first by platform and lists the desktop wallet, the mobile wallet, the web wallet and the hardware signing device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The platform determines how convenient the wallet is, how exposed it is to attack, and how much of the user's data is revealed to others.

Every platform trades one benefit against another. A desktop wallet gives control and autonomy but runs on a general-purpose computer; a mobile wallet is convenient but often relies on remote servers; a web wallet is the easiest to start with and gives up the most control; a hardware device offers the strongest protection of keys and needs a second program to do the rest. Knowing the pattern lets a learner judge any new wallet, not only the ones named in the book.

The four concepts of this section follow the order of the chapter. Each is described by what it runs on, what it protects, and what the user must trust. The comparison rests on the facts the chapter gives, and the remaining sections of the branch add the two other classifications of autonomy and key control.

nodes.label: Desktop wallet
nodes.body: A desktop wallet is a wallet program that runs on a personal computer. The chapter says that it was the first type of Bitcoin wallet created as a reference implementation, and that many users run desktop wallets for the features, autonomy and control they offer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The operating systems it runs on are general-use ones such as Windows and macOS.

paras.text: A desktop wallet is a wallet program that runs on a personal computer. The chapter says that it was the first type of Bitcoin wallet created as a reference implementation, and that many users run desktop wallets for the features, autonomy and control they offer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The operating systems it runs on are general-use ones such as Windows and macOS.

The desktop wallet matters because it is the platform on which a user can run a full node and thereby need to trust nobody else. The chapter groups the desktop full node among the most common arrangements and notes that in it you control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Features that smaller devices cannot offer are also found here, such as the use of the wallet together with a node that validates the entire history.

The reference implementation of Bitcoin, discussed in chapter 3 of the book, is a desktop program that includes a wallet, and many other desktop wallets exist. The chapter contrasts the desktop wallet with the mobile wallet, the type it calls the most common, and with the web wallet that is used through a browser (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The wallet runs as an ordinary application of the operating system. It stores its keys and its database on the computer's disk, and it connects to the network either as a full node or through another program. Because of this, the security of the money depends on the security of the whole computer: the chapter points out that running on general-use operating systems such as Windows and macOS has certain security disadvantages, as these platforms are often insecure and poorly configured (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Autonomy and control come at a price in responsibility. A desktop wallet protects nothing if the computer carries malicious software, and a lost or damaged disk loses the keys unless a backup exists. A student should therefore treat the desktop wallet as a choice for users who accept those duties, and should not assume that a program on a personal computer is more secure than a service run by professionals.

nodes.definition: The first type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a general-purpose operating system such as Windows or macOS.

nodes.label: Mobile wallet
nodes.body: A mobile wallet is a wallet application on a smartphone. The chapter calls it the most common type of Bitcoin wallet and says that it runs on smartphone operating systems such as Apple iOS and Android (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's first wallet in the chapter's story is of this type: she downloads one of Joe's recommendations and installs it on her phone.

paras.text: A mobile wallet is a wallet application on a smartphone. The chapter calls it the most common type of Bitcoin wallet and says that it runs on smartphone operating systems such as Apple iOS and Android (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Alice's first wallet in the chapter's story is of this type: she downloads one of Joe's recommendations and installs it on her phone.

The phone is the device that people carry and use for everything, so a wallet on it is the natural way to receive and spend small amounts. The chapter describes these wallets as often a great choice for new users, many being designed for simplicity and ease of use, while there are also fully featured mobile wallets for power users (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The scenes of the chapter that happen on a screen use a mobile wallet: Alice's Receive button that shows a QR code, Joe's Send button that opens a QR scanner, and the screen on which the amount and fee are entered (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The camera of the phone and its screen make the QR code a natural way to hand over an address.

To avoid downloading and storing large amounts of data, the chapter explains, most mobile wallets retrieve information from remote servers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is the design of a lightweight client: the phone keeps the keys and creates the transactions, but depends on another computer for information about the chain. The next section of the branch, on node types, explains the consequences.

The convenience has a privacy cost. The chapter warns that retrieving information from remote servers reduces your privacy by disclosing to third parties information about your Bitcoin addresses and balances (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second consideration is that a phone can be lost, stolen or reset, which is why the chapter follows the creation of the wallet at once with the recovery code.

nodes.definition: The most common type of Bitcoin wallet, run on a smartphone operating system such as iOS or Android.

nodes.label: Web wallet
nodes.body: A web wallet is a wallet that is accessed through a web browser and stores the user's wallet on a server owned by a third party. The chapter compares it to webmail, because it relies entirely on a third-party server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The user types into a page what a desktop or mobile user would do in an application.

paras.text: A web wallet is a wallet that is accessed through a web browser and stores the user's wallet on a server owned by a third party. The chapter compares it to webmail, because it relies entirely on a third-party server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The user types into a page what a desktop or mobile user would do in an application.

Web wallets are easy to start with, which is why they are popular, and they show the central trade-off of the chapter in its clearest form: simplicity against control. The chapter notes that most web wallets take control of the Bitcoin keys from users in exchange for ease of use, and that it is inadvisable to store large amounts of bitcoin on third-party systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The web-based account with a third party is one of the three common groups the chapter lists, and it is the one in which you do not control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Exchanges and other services that hold balances for their customers behave in this way. The next sections of the branch name the arrangement custodial and describe its opposite.

The wallet's data lives on a server that the provider runs. Some of these services operate using client-side code running in the user's browser, which keeps control of the Bitcoin keys in the hands of the user, although the user's dependence on the server still compromises their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Most do not do so, and a service that holds the keys can move the funds on its own.

Convenience and safety should not be confused. A page in a browser looks like any other page, and the user cannot easily see whether the keys are on his device or on the provider's server. The advice of the chapter is plain: do not keep large amounts on third-party systems, and remember that dependence on the server reveals information about the user even in the best case.

nodes.definition: A wallet used through a web browser, whose data usually lives on a server owned by a third party.

nodes.label: Hardware signing device
nodes.body: A hardware signing device is a small device that stores keys and signs transactions using special-purpose hardware and software built into the device. The chapter says that such devices usually connect to a desktop, mobile or web wallet by a cable, by a short-range wireless link, or by a camera that reads QR codes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are sometimes called hardware wallets, but the chapter prefers the longer name for a reason it states.

paras.text: A hardware signing device is a small device that stores keys and signs transactions using special-purpose hardware and software built into the device. The chapter says that such devices usually connect to a desktop, mobile or web wallet by a cable, by a short-range wireless link, or by a camera that reads QR codes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They are sometimes called hardware wallets, but the chapter prefers the longer name for a reason it states.

The purpose is to keep the private key away from the computer or phone that is most exposed to attack. By handling all Bitcoin-related operations on the specialised hardware, the chapter says, these wallets are less vulnerable to many types of attacks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A device that only signs, and never shows the key, reduces the damage that malicious software on the connected computer can do.

The device is used together with another wallet. The chapter stresses that it needs to be paired with a full-featured wallet to send and receive transactions, and that the security and privacy offered by that paired wallet play a critical role in how much security and privacy the user obtains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice the paired wallet prepares the transaction, the device signs it, and the paired wallet sends it.

The flow follows from the idea of the digital signature. The wallet shows the transaction to the device; the device signs it with the private key stored inside, which never leaves the hardware; the signed transaction goes back to the wallet and on to the network. The device therefore needs only to hold keys and to sign, and the rest of the wallet's work stays on the paired program.

The name hardware wallet is misleading, and the chapter says so in its own way: the device does not hold bitcoin, nor does it see the network, and it needs a second wallet. Its protection is limited to the keys. A student should also remember that the device is used with a recovery code, since a lost device has to be replaceable, and that the privacy of the paired wallet remains the privacy of the user.

nodes.example: a device that stores keys and signs
nodes.definition: A hardware signing device stores keys and signs transactions with special-purpose hardware; it must be paired with a full-featured wallet to send and receive.

nodes.label: Node type
nodes.body: The node type of a wallet describes how much of the network's work the wallet does for itself. The chapter's section Full node versus Lightweight classifies wallets by their degree of autonomy and by how they interact with the Bitcoin network, and distinguishes the full node, the lightweight client and the third-party API client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fourth concept of the section explains the words peer and client that the chapter uses to describe the arrangement.

paras.text: The node type of a wallet describes how much of the network's work the wallet does for itself. The chapter's section Full node versus Lightweight classifies wallets by their degree of autonomy and by how they interact with the Bitcoin network, and distinguishes the full node, the lightweight client and the third-party API client (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fourth concept of the section explains the words peer and client that the chapter uses to describe the arrangement.

Autonomy decides whom the user has to trust. A program that validates everything itself trusts nobody, a program that checks only part of the data trusts its sources for the rest, and a program that asks a remote service trusts that service completely. The three degrees line up with three levels of resource use, from heavy to light.

The section orders the node types from the most autonomous to the least. The full node validates the entire history. The lightweight client keeps the wallet locally and validates partially. The third-party API client trusts a remote system for accurate information and for its privacy. The final concept, peers and clients, names the roles in the peer-to-peer network that these three types play.

nodes.label: Full node
nodes.body: A full node is a program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions, every transaction by every user, ever. The chapter adds that, optionally, full nodes can also store previously validated transactions and serve data to other Bitcoin programs, either on the same computer or over the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node therefore does not take anyone's word for what has happened.

paras.text: A full node is a program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions, every transaction by every user, ever. The chapter adds that, optionally, full nodes can also store previously validated transactions and serve data to other Bitcoin programs, either on the same computer or over the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A full node therefore does not take anyone's word for what has happened.

The full node is the one that gives the user complete autonomy, which is the chapter's term for needing to trust no one else. The price is resources: the chapter estimates that a full node uses about the same computer resources as watching an hour-long streaming video for each day of Bitcoin transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper had foreseen the arrangement, and notes that businesses that receive frequent payments will probably still want to run their own nodes for more independent security and quicker verification (Nakamoto, 2008).

Full nodes are the peers of the network. The chapter's note on peers and clients says that full nodes are the peers: each peer individually validates every confirmed transaction and can provide data to its user with complete authority (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reference implementation, Bitcoin Core, can be run as a full node, and chapter 3 of the book describes how.

A full node starts by obtaining the blocks of the chain from other nodes and checks each one against the rules of the protocol; it keeps only those that pass. Because it checks everything for itself, it can later tell its wallet, without trusting anyone, whether a payment has really been confirmed. The whitepaper's description is that nodes accept a block only if all transactions in it are valid and not already spent (Nakamoto, 2008).

A full node is not necessarily a miner and not necessarily a wallet; it validates, and these other roles are added separately. It also does not make a payment faster or the network larger by itself. Its value is for its operator and for the network as a whole, since the more independent nodes check the rules, the harder it is to change the rules by force. A last point is that running one needs patience: the first download of the whole history takes a long time.

nodes.definition: A program that validates the entire history of Bitcoin transactions itself and may serve data to other programs.

nodes.label: Lightweight client
nodes.body: A lightweight client, also known as a simplified-payment-verification (SPV) client, connects to a full node or other remote server for receiving and sending Bitcoin transaction information, but stores the user wallet locally, partially validates the transactions it receives, and independently creates outgoing transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the middle form between the full node and the client that trusts a remote service entirely.

paras.text: A lightweight client, also known as a simplified-payment-verification (SPV) client, connects to a full node or other remote server for receiving and sending Bitcoin transaction information, but stores the user wallet locally, partially validates the transactions it receives, and independently creates outgoing transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the middle form between the full node and the client that trusts a remote service entirely.

Most users cannot or will not run a full node on a phone, and the lightweight client is the practical answer. It keeps the one thing that cannot be delegated, the keys, and delegates the heavy task of storing and checking the chain. The whitepaper describes the method: a user needs only a copy of the block headers of the longest proof-of-work chain and a short proof that links a transaction to the block in which it is time-stamped (Nakamoto, 2008).

The mobile lightweight wallet is one of the three most common arrangements named in the chapter, and in it you control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The connection to a remote server is the reason mobile wallets disclose information about addresses and balances to third parties, as the chapter notes in the section on mobile wallets.

The client cannot check the transaction for itself; by linking it to a place in the chain, the whitepaper says, the client sees that a network node has accepted it, and blocks added after it further confirm that the network has accepted it (Nakamoto, 2008). The verification is reliable as long as honest nodes control the network and is more vulnerable if an attacker overpowers it, because the simplified method can be fooled by fabricated transactions for as long as the attacker can continue to overpower the network.

A lightweight client reduces its dependence on any single server by connecting to several peers, but the chapter is clear about the limit: the security of a client ultimately relies on the integrity of its peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A student should therefore read lightweight as a statement about validation and not about control: the client still holds the keys and still creates its own transactions.

nodes.definition: A client that keeps the wallet locally but relies on a full node or server for most data and validates only partly.

nodes.label: Third-party API client
nodes.body: A third-party API client is a wallet that interacts with Bitcoin through the interfaces of a third-party system, instead of connecting to the Bitcoin network directly. The chapter adds that the wallet may be stored by the user or by third-party servers, but that the client trusts the remote server to provide it with accurate information and to protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The interface in question is an application programming interface, a concept explained in the Foundations branch.

paras.text: A third-party API client is a wallet that interacts with Bitcoin through the interfaces of a third-party system, instead of connecting to the Bitcoin network directly. The chapter adds that the wallet may be stored by the user or by third-party servers, but that the client trusts the remote server to provide it with accurate information and to protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The interface in question is an application programming interface, a concept explained in the Foundations branch.

This type is the least autonomous of the three, and it is included so that a student can see the whole range. A program that reads everything from a remote service has no means of checking that service. If the service is wrong, hacked or dishonest, the client cannot know, and the service learns what the client asks.

Many web and mobile applications work this way, and so do services that offer an interface for developers. The programming interface is the contract between the application that offers a service and other software that uses it (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). A wallet of this kind is, in effect, a window onto someone else's node.

The client sends requests to the remote service, such as the balance of an address or the data of a transaction, and receives answers that it displays. It does not verify the answers against the chain, since it has no copy. The key difference from the lightweight client is that the lightweight client checks part of what it receives and talks to the network; this client checks nothing and talks to a service.

The trust placed in the remote server is complete. The chapter says that the client trusts the remote server to provide accurate information and to protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and these two trusts can fail independently. If the keys are also held by the third party, the arrangement becomes a custodial one, which the next branch of the chapter treats.

nodes.example: a client of a remote service
nodes.definition: A third-party API client uses a remote system's programming interface instead of the Bitcoin network and trusts it for correct information and privacy.

nodes.label: Peer and client
nodes.body: Peer and client are the two roles in the Bitcoin network, in the chapter's words. Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network, and the full nodes are the peers: each peer individually validates every confirmed transaction and can provide data to its user with complete authority. Lightweight wallets and other software are clients: each client depends on one or more peers to provide it with valid data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Peer and client are the two roles in the Bitcoin network, in the chapter's words. Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network, and the full nodes are the peers: each peer individually validates every confirmed transaction and can provide data to its user with complete authority. Lightweight wallets and other software are clients: each client depends on one or more peers to provide it with valid data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The distinction explains where trust lies. A peer trusts its own checking, whereas a client trusts its peers. A general definition from the vocabulary of the internet agrees: a client is a system entity that requests and uses a service provided by another, called a server (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin the roles are more symmetrical, because every peer is also a server of data to others.

The words appear in the note that the chapter gives at the end of the node types. Bitcoin clients can perform secondary validation on some of the data they receive and make connections to multiple peers to reduce their dependence on the integrity of a single peer, but the security of a client ultimately relies on the integrity of its peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same vocabulary is used in the descriptions of the network in later chapters.

A peer-to-peer network has no server at its centre: each node can ask for data and give data. A client such as a phone wallet connects to one or more peers and asks them what it needs. When several peers answer the same, the client's confidence increases; when they disagree, the client has a reason to look further. The mechanism is a modest one, and the chapter does not oversell it.

A client is not worse than a peer in every way: it can be much cheaper to run, and it still holds its own keys. The point is that its safety depends on someone else's honesty. A student should not describe the network as if every user were a peer, because most users, running wallets on phones, are clients.

nodes.example: full nodes as peers, wallets as clients
nodes.definition: In the peer-to-peer network, full nodes are the peers and lightweight wallets are clients that depend on one or more peers for valid data.

nodes.label: Key control
nodes.body: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. If you are the only one with control over the keys, you are in control of your bitcoins; if you do not have control, your bitcoins are managed by a third party who ultimately controls your funds on your behalf (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Key control is the question of who holds the private keys that unlock a wallet's funds. The chapter calls this a very important additional consideration and says that access to bitcoins is controlled by private keys, which are like very long PINs. If you are the only one with control over the keys, you are in control of your bitcoins; if you do not have control, your bitcoins are managed by a third party who ultimately controls your funds on your behalf (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The question decides who really owns the money. In the traditional financial system a bank holds the account and the customer holds a claim against it, whereas in Bitcoin the holder of the key holds the money itself. The chapter condenses the lesson into the sentence Your keys, your coins. Not your keys, not your coins, which its author says he coined to emphasise this point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Two concepts divide the section. The noncustodial wallet is the arrangement in which the user alone controls the keys and bears the responsibility for backing them up. The custodial wallet or account is the arrangement in which a custodian holds the keys. The chapter's advice is to understand the difference before choosing, since the same word wallet is used for both.

nodes.label: Noncustodial wallet
nodes.body: A noncustodial wallet is a wallet in which the user, and only the user, controls the keys. In the story of the chapter, the wallet that Alice has chosen is a noncustodial wallet, so Alice (and only Alice) will be in control of her keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word custodial refers to a custodian, a third party who holds something on behalf of its owner; the prefix non- means that there is none.

paras.text: A noncustodial wallet is a wallet in which the user, and only the user, controls the keys. In the story of the chapter, the wallet that Alice has chosen is a noncustodial wallet, so Alice (and only Alice) will be in control of her keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word custodial refers to a custodian, a third party who holds something on behalf of its owner; the prefix non- means that there is none.

Control of the key is the only prerequisite to spending: possession of the key that can sign a transaction is, according to the chapter, the only thing required to spend bitcoin, which puts the control entirely in the hands of each user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same fact has a hard consequence, which the chapter states at once: Alice bears responsibility for backing the keys up, since losing the keys means she loses access to her bitcoins.

The noncustodial wallet is the kind that the chapter treats as the basic case. Desktop full nodes and mobile lightweight wallets are the two groups in which you control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The recovery code that the wallet produces is the instrument by which the user takes up the responsibility.

The wallet creates the private keys on the user's device, keeps them there, and signs transactions on request. No server needs to approve a payment, and none can block one. When the device is lost, a noncustodial wallet can be restored from the recovery code, which the next section describes; without it, nobody can help, because nobody else holds the keys.

Freedom from a third party is also freedom from its protection. There is no password reset, no support desk that can restore access, and no insurer. A student who recommends a noncustodial wallet to a beginner should recommend the backup with it. The chapter also warns that the real danger is fraud, since malware that mimics a wallet can trick the user into giving the code away.

nodes.definition: A wallet where only the user holds the keys, so only the user controls and can lose the bitcoin.

nodes.label: Custodial wallet
nodes.body: A custodial wallet, or account with a custodian, is the opposite of the noncustodial wallet: a third party controls the keys. The chapter divides key management software into two important categories based on control, wallets, where you control the keys, and the funds and accounts with custodians, where some third party controls the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The custodian then manages the user's funds on his behalf.

paras.text: A custodial wallet, or account with a custodian, is the opposite of the noncustodial wallet: a third party controls the keys. The chapter divides key management software into two important categories based on control, wallets, where you control the keys, and the funds and accounts with custodians, where some third party controls the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The custodian then manages the user's funds on his behalf.

Custody is convenient, and for that reason it is common. The user does not have to look after a backup or fear the loss of a device. The chapter lists web-based accounts with third parties as one of the three common groups of wallets, and says explicitly that in it you do not control the keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The price is that the bitcoin is in effect a claim on the custodian.

Exchanges that hold balances for customers, and web services that store a wallet on their own server, are custodians. The chapter also uses the phrase when it advises that it is inadvisable to store large amounts of bitcoin on third-party systems (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A Bitcoin ATM that sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet delivers the money to the user's own keys, which is the point where custody ends.

The custodian keeps the keys in its own systems and maintains an account for each customer in its own records. A payment between two customers of the same custodian may not touch the Bitcoin network at all. The customer proves his identity to the custodian, not to the network, usually with a password, and the custodian signs the transactions that move the funds.

The risk lies with the custodian: if it fails, is hacked, or refuses a withdrawal, the customer has only a claim against it. The first sentence of the chapter's slogan states the remedy, and the second one states the cost. A fair reading is neither that custody is always wrong nor that it is safe, but that the user should know which arrangement he is in and how much he is willing to trust.

nodes.definition: A custodial wallet or account is one where a third party, the custodian, holds the keys and manages the funds for the user.

nodes.label: Backup
nodes.body: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong. It begins with the chapter's account of Alice's first start-up, when her noncustodial wallet produces a recovery code that can be used to restore it, and it goes on to the additional data that a recovery code does not contain, and to the payments that some technologies keep outside the public blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Backup section is about getting a wallet back after something goes wrong. It begins with the chapter's account of Alice's first start-up, when her noncustodial wallet produces a recovery code that can be used to restore it, and it goes on to the additional data that a recovery code does not contain, and to the payments that some technologies keep outside the public blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In a system without a helpdesk, the backup is the only insurance. The chapter explains that the control of the keys brings the responsibility for them, and that a user who loses the keys loses the money. The section therefore treats the recovery code, the wallet's other data, and the newer payment methods in turn, because each has its own way of being lost.

The recovery code is the central concept, and the section also covers wallet metadata, the labels and notes of the user. The offchain payment is described in the Usage branch, because it is a way of paying; the section draws the consequence for backup. The warning about fake wallets that ask for the code belongs to the recovery code, and is explained there.

nodes.label: Recovery code
nodes.body: A recovery code is a short secret, created by the wallet, from which all of the wallet's keys can be rebuilt. The chapter says that most modern noncustodial Bitcoin wallets will provide a recovery code for their user to back up, that it usually consists of numbers, letters or words selected randomly by the software, and that it is used as the basis for the keys that are generated by the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is sometimes called a mnemonic or a seed phrase.

paras.text: A recovery code is a short secret, created by the wallet, from which all of the wallet's keys can be rebuilt. The chapter says that most modern noncustodial Bitcoin wallets will provide a recovery code for their user to back up, that it usually consists of numbers, letters or words selected randomly by the software, and that it is used as the basis for the keys that are generated by the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is sometimes called a mnemonic or a seed phrase.

The code makes the backup practical. A wallet contains many keys, and each new address uses a new one, but a single short code can restore them all. The chapter explains that if something happens to Alice's wallet she can download a new copy of her wallet software and enter this recovery code to rebuild the wallet database of all the onchain transactions she has ever sent or received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other names reflect its role: seed phrase, because it provides the input, the seed, to the function that generates all of a wallet's keys.

The chapter shows three samples. The wallet BlueWallet gives twelve numbered words, the Electrum wallet gives twelve words, and the Muun wallet gives eight groups of four letters and digits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A widely deployed convention for such word lists is BIP 39, which describes a mnemonic sentence of 12 to 24 words for the generation of deterministic wallets and calls a sentence of easy-to-remember words superior for human interaction to raw binary or hexadecimal values (Palatinus et al., 2013).

In the BIP 39 convention, the wallet first generates random bits called the initial entropy, between 128 and 256 bits. It appends a checksum made from the first ENT/32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the entropy, splits the whole into groups of 11 bits, and uses each group as an index into a list of 2048 words; for 128 bits of entropy this gives (128 + 4) / 11 = 12 words (Palatinus et al., 2013). To turn the words into a binary seed, the standard runs a key-stretching function, PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 and 2048 iterations, whose result is 512 bits, or 64 bytes. The same words with the same passphrase therefore always lead to the same seed and to the same keys, and that is what makes recovery possible. The example counts the words of the Electrum sample from the chapter: 12.

The code is the key to the money, and whoever sees it can take the funds, so it must be kept offline and private. The chapter's warning is explicit: malware applications mimic the design of a wallet, insist that you enter your recovery code, and relay it to the developer so that they can steal your funds, which is the equivalent of phishing websites. Most wallets ask for the code only at the initial set-up and during recovery; if an application asks at any other time, the chapter advises consulting an expert (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also notes that writing the phrase down on paper tends to be more reliable than memory, and that the code alone does not restore data such as labels.

nodes.definition: A recovery code of words, numbers or letters chosen at random by the wallet, from which all its keys are generated and from which the wallet can be restored.
