nodes.label: Lightning Network
nodes.body: The Lightning Network is a network of payment channels. The glossary of the textbook describes it as a proposed implementation of Hashed Timelock Contracts with bi-directional payment channels, which allows payments to be securely routed across multiple peer-to-peer payment channels, so that any peer on the network can pay any other even if they do not directly have a channel open between each other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its authors' paper presents the idea as a way to scale Bitcoin by moving most payments off the chain (Poon and Dryja, 2016).

paras.text: The Lightning Network is a network of payment channels. The glossary of the textbook describes it as a proposed implementation of Hashed Timelock Contracts with bi-directional payment channels, which allows payments to be securely routed across multiple peer-to-peer payment channels, so that any peer on the network can pay any other even if they do not directly have a channel open between each other (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its authors' paper presents the idea as a way to scale Bitcoin by moving most payments off the chain (Poon and Dryja, 2016).

A single channel only helps two parties who deal with each other often. By linking channels into a network, the system lets a payer reach people with whom he has no channel, in the way that the internet lets any computer reach any other through intermediate machines. This extends the benefits of offchain payment, lower cost and better privacy, to ordinary payments between strangers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter mentions the Lightning Network only twice, in the glossary entry and in the discussion of offchain payments, and the later chapters of the book return to it in detail; this course therefore treats it here as a named example of offchain technology and not as a subject of its own. It is met today in wallets that offer fast payments with low fees beside ordinary onchain ones, and in the payment pages of merchants who accept both. Its own authors present it as a way of carrying a large volume of payments without writing each of them into the chain (Poon and Dryja, 2016).

A payer finds a path of channels from himself to the recipient, and each intermediate party forwards the payment over its own channel. The example has channels Alice-Bob, Bob-Carol and Carol-Dave. There is no direct channel between Alice and Dave, but the program finds the route Alice, Bob, Carol, Dave, of three hops.

A routed payment depends on the intermediaries having enough funds in the right channels, and it is a different system from the chain: it has its own failures and its own privacy and backup considerations. Funds held in channels are not visible in the blockchain, so a wallet that supports the network needs its database backed up as well as its recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: The Lightning Network connects payment channels so that a payment can be routed through several of them, and any peer can pay any other even without a direct channel.

nodes.label: Electronic payment
nodes.body: An electronic payment is a payment made through an electronic network instead of with cash. The chapter names the common forms: most electronic payment networks, such as credit cards, debit cards, PayPal and bank account transfers, are reversible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Conventional money is also often stored and transmitted digitally, and in those cases the counterfeiting and double-spend issues are handled by clearing all electronic transactions through central authorities that have a global view of the currency in circulation.

paras.text: An electronic payment is a payment made through an electronic network instead of with cash. The chapter names the common forms: most electronic payment networks, such as credit cards, debit cards, PayPal and bank account transfers, are reversible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Conventional money is also often stored and transmitted digitally, and in those cases the counterfeiting and double-spend issues are handled by clearing all electronic transactions through central authorities that have a global view of the currency in circulation.

The comparison with electronic payments explains two features of Bitcoin. First, reversibility is a service that central institutions can provide because they can see and change the record, and Bitcoin has no such institution. Second, the difference creates a risk that is central to buying bitcoin: for someone selling bitcoin, a reversible payment introduces a very high risk that the buyer will reverse the electronic payment after receiving the bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Electronic payments are what a new user uses to acquire a first bitcoin, at an exchange or through another company. The chapter notes that companies accepting traditional electronic payments in return for bitcoin usually require identity verification and credit-worthiness checks, which may take several days or weeks, so that a new user cannot buy bitcoin instantly with a credit card (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A card or bank payment passes through intermediaries that record and can reverse it. The seller of bitcoin can protect himself only by checking the buyer and by waiting, because once the bitcoin has been sent it cannot be taken back. The whitepaper explains the underlying economics: the possibility of reversal makes merchants wary of customers and increases the cost of transactions (Nakamoto, 2008).

Reversible does not mean better or worse; it means that the risk sits with a different party. Reversibility protects a buyer who has been cheated and exposes a seller to the fraud of a reversed payment, while irreversibility does the opposite, and the whitepaper proposes to balance the second case by a routine escrow arrangement in which a third party holds the money until both sides agree (Nakamoto, 2008). The chapter's lesson for a student is therefore practical rather than moral: before acting, establish which kind of payment is involved, because the party who can be hurt by a mistake is not the same in the two cases. It is also the reason that the chapter's four ways of acquiring bitcoin differ so much in how long they take.

nodes.definition: An electronic payment is a payment made over an electronic network; credit cards, debit cards, PayPal and bank transfers are reversible, unlike Bitcoin transactions.

nodes.label: Semantic bridge
nodes.body: The semantic bridge connects the chapter's central idea with the theme of this course, semantic technologies. The idea is that control belongs to whoever holds the keys, with no central registry that grants or removes it. The World Wide Web Consortium has turned the same idea into standards for digital identity, the Decentralized Identifiers and the Verifiable Credentials (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

paras.text: The semantic bridge connects the chapter's central idea with the theme of this course, semantic technologies. The idea is that control belongs to whoever holds the keys, with no central registry that grants or removes it. The World Wide Web Consortium has turned the same idea into standards for digital identity, the Decentralized Identifiers and the Verifiable Credentials (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

A student of blockchain technology should know that its main principle is not limited to money. Whenever a system needs to say who someone is, or what someone may do, it faces the same choice between a central registry and control by keys. The bridge shows that the choice recurs in the identity layer of the web, and that standard vocabularies exist for it.

Two concepts form the bridge. A decentralized identifier is an identifier that its holder controls without a central registry. A verifiable credential is a set of claims about a subject that an issuer has signed and that a holder can show to a verifier. Both are specified as W3C Recommendations, and both rely on the digital signatures and keys explained in the Foundations branch.

nodes.label: Decentralized identifier
nodes.body: A decentralized identifier, abbreviated DID, is a new type of identifier that enables verifiable, decentralized digital identity. The W3C Recommendation of 19 July 2022 says that a DID refers to any subject, such as a person, an organisation or a thing, as determined by the controller of the DID (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). It is a standard way to name something and to let its controller prove that he controls the name.

paras.text: A decentralized identifier, abbreviated DID, is a new type of identifier that enables verifiable, decentralized digital identity. The W3C Recommendation of 19 July 2022 says that a DID refers to any subject, such as a person, an organisation or a thing, as determined by the controller of the DID (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). It is a standard way to name something and to let its controller prove that he controls the name.

The aim is independence from central parties. The specification says that, in contrast to typical federated identifiers, DIDs have been designed so that they may be decoupled from centralized registries, identity providers and certificate authorities, and that the design enables the controller of a DID to prove control over it without requiring permission from any other party (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). This is the principle of the chapter, control by whoever holds the keys, applied to identity.

DIDs are met in digital identity wallets, in credentials for education and employment, and in research on self-sovereign identity. Each DID is a URI that associates a DID subject with a DID document, which can express cryptographic material and verification methods, so that interactions associated with that subject can be trusted (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). The standard is independent of any particular blockchain.

A DID is resolved to a DID document that lists, among other things, public keys. The controller demonstrates control by producing a digital signature that can be checked with a key from the document, much as a Bitcoin user shows control of an address by signing a transaction with the matching private key. The relation between identifier and key, and not a record in a database, is what carries the identity.

A DID is not a credential and does not say who a person is; it says only that whoever controls it can prove it. The claims that give an identifier meaning, such as an education certificate, come from the verifiable credentials of the next concept. A second caution is that the standard does not require a blockchain, and the use of the Bitcoin idea in a DID method is a design choice that each method makes for itself.

nodes.example: a DID controlled by its holder
nodes.definition: A W3C Decentralized Identifier is an identifier that its controller can prove control over without a central registry, applying the principle of control by keys to identity.

nodes.label: Verifiable credential
nodes.body: A verifiable credential is a specific way to express a set of claims made by an issuer, such as a driver's license or an education certificate. The W3C Recommendation of 15 May 2025 describes an extensible data model for such credentials, ways to secure them from tampering, and a three-party ecosystem composed of issuers, holders and verifiers (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025).

paras.text: A verifiable credential is a specific way to express a set of claims made by an issuer, such as a driver's license or an education certificate. The W3C Recommendation of 15 May 2025 describes an extensible data model for such credentials, ways to secure them from tampering, and a three-party ecosystem composed of issuers, holders and verifiers (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025).

Credentials are what make an identifier useful. The specification says that a verifiable credential can represent all the same information that a physical credential represents, and that technologies such as digital signatures can make it more tamper-evident and trustworthy than its physical counterpart (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025). The same family of ideas, signatures that prove origin and integrity, secures Bitcoin transactions.

Credentials appear in university diplomas, professional licences and access passes. The roles are the following: the issuer creates and signs the credential, the holder keeps it and presents it, and the verifier checks it. Holders can generate verifiable presentations and share them with verifiers to prove that they possess credentials with specific characteristics (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025).

The flow follows the signature mechanism that the Foundations branch explains. The issuer signs the claims with its private key; the verifier checks the signature with the issuer's public key and so learns that the claims come from the issuer and have not been altered. Nobody needs to ask the issuer in the moment of checking. This is how a diploma can be checked without calling the university.

A valid signature shows that the issuer made the claim, not that the claim is true. A verifier still has to decide whether to trust the issuer. The specification also treats privacy as a design issue, and a careless presentation can reveal more than the verifier needs. In this course the standard serves as a bridge to semantic technologies and not as a feature of Bitcoin itself.

nodes.definition: A verifiable credential expresses claims made by an issuer, such as a driver's licence or education certificate, in a form protected by digital signatures that a holder can present to a verifier.

nodes.label: Acquisition
nodes.body: The Acquisition section lists the ways in which a newcomer obtains a first bitcoin, which is the practical problem a reader faces as soon as the wallet is installed. The chapter says that the first task for new users is to acquire some bitcoin, and it names four methods: finding a friend who has some and buying directly, earning bitcoin by selling a product or a service, using a Bitcoin ATM in one's city, and using a currency exchange linked to a bank account (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fifth concept of the section explains the identity checks that accompany some of these, because the chapter devotes a paragraph to why they exist and how long they take.

paras.text: The Acquisition section lists the ways in which a newcomer obtains a first bitcoin, which is the practical problem a reader faces as soon as the wallet is installed. The chapter says that the first task for new users is to acquire some bitcoin, and it names four methods: finding a friend who has some and buying directly, earning bitcoin by selling a product or a service, using a Bitcoin ATM in one's city, and using a currency exchange linked to a bank account (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A fifth concept of the section explains the identity checks that accompany some of these, because the chapter devotes a paragraph to why they exist and how long they take.

Acquisition is the point at which Bitcoin touches the conventional financial system, and the chapter spends a whole section on it because the two systems behave differently where they meet. Conventional electronic payments are reversible and regulated, while bitcoin payments are irreversible, and the chapter draws the consequence: a seller of bitcoin who accepts a reversible payment carries a very high risk, which is why companies demand identity and credit checks that may take days or weeks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The four methods therefore differ not only in convenience but in how private they are, how quickly they work, and how much of the conventional system a newcomer has to enter in order to use them.

The four methods can be read as a scale from the least to the most formal. A friend sells directly, with nothing between the two people but an agreed rate; a worker or a shop is paid in bitcoin for something of value; a machine takes cash and sends bitcoin to a phone; and an exchange offers a market with a bank account behind it. The chapter's own summary of the first method is that it is the least complicated, and it suggests a local Bitcoin meetup as a way to find such a seller (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The concept of identity verification then explains why the more formal methods ask for documents, and the privacy concept of the address group explains why that matters for everything the buyer does afterwards.

nodes.label: Buy from friend
nodes.body: Buying from a friend means obtaining bitcoin directly from a person who already has some. The chapter describes the method in a single instruction: find a friend who has bitcoins and buy some from him or her directly, adding that many Bitcoin users start this way and that this method is the least complicated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the method that Alice uses in the chapter's story, when she buys 0.001 bitcoin from Joe for cash.

paras.text: Buying from a friend means obtaining bitcoin directly from a person who already has some. The chapter describes the method in a single instruction: find a friend who has bitcoins and buy some from him or her directly, adding that many Bitcoin users start this way and that this method is the least complicated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the method that Alice uses in the chapter's story, when she buys 0.001 bitcoin from Joe for cash.

The method avoids the delay and the checks of the formal routes. Because bitcoin transactions are irreversible, a seller who accepts a reversible card payment bears a very high risk, and companies therefore ask for identity verification, which may take several days or weeks; the chapter says that as a new user you cannot buy bitcoin instantly with a credit card (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A friend who accepts cash, or a transfer between friends, avoids most of that.

The chapter suggests one way to meet people with bitcoin: attend a local Bitcoin meetup listed on Meetup.com (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The scene with Alice and Joe at a party shows the other, informal route. The exchange in the story takes a few minutes: they agree on a price, Alice pays in cash, and Joe sends the bitcoin to her address.

The two sides first settle the price, using a current market rate as explained in the Price section, then settle the payment in cash or another way they trust, and finally the seller sends the bitcoin from his wallet to the address that the buyer displays. The buyer sees the incoming payment in her wallet within seconds. The seller's risk is small when the payment is made in cash in person.

A friend is not a guarantee. The amounts in a private deal are not protected by a regulated intermediary, and the buyer must check that the address is her own and that the payment arrives. If the transfer is later found to be a mistake, nobody can reverse it. The method also offers only small, occasional amounts and is not a supply for regular use.

nodes.definition: The least complicated way to get a first bitcoin: buy directly from someone who has some.

nodes.label: Earn bitcoin
nodes.body: Earning bitcoin means being paid in bitcoin for work or goods. The chapter gives the method in two examples: earn bitcoin by selling a product or service for bitcoin; if you are a programmer, sell your programming skills; if you are a hairdresser, cut hair for bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The method obtains bitcoin without buying it.

paras.text: Earning bitcoin means being paid in bitcoin for work or goods. The chapter gives the method in two examples: earn bitcoin by selling a product or service for bitcoin; if you are a programmer, sell your programming skills; if you are a hairdresser, cut hair for bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The method obtains bitcoin without buying it.

It is the method that fits the vision of the chapter most closely, in which Bitcoin is a currency for ordinary commerce. The opening pages say that users can transfer bitcoin to do just about anything that can be done with conventional currencies, including buying and selling goods, sending money to people or organisations, or extending credit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A person who earns bitcoin never meets the reversible payment networks that cause the delays.

A freelancer, a shop and a service provider who accept bitcoin are the everyday examples, and the chapter's own two are a programmer who sells programming skills and a hairdresser who cuts hair for bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The seller needs very little: an address or an invoice to give to the customer and a wallet to receive the payment, both of which the chapter's opening story already produced. The opening pages add how wide the range of such uses is, since users can transfer bitcoin to do just about anything that can be done with conventional currencies, including buying and selling goods, sending money to people or organisations, and extending credit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Merchants in the later chapters of the book use payment processors to do the same thing at a larger scale.

The seller creates an invoice, which includes the address, the amount and a description, the customer pays, and the seller waits for the confirmations that he considers sufficient for the value of the goods. Because payment cannot be reversed by the payer, the seller is spared the fraud that card payments allow, but must take care that the price in bitcoin follows the current exchange rate.

Income in bitcoin has the same exposure to price changes as any holding: the value of the amount received in a national currency can rise or fall before it is spent. A seller who must pay costs in a national currency may decide to convert at once. Rules on taxes and reporting apply in many countries, and this textbook does not describe them.

nodes.example: payment for a product or service
nodes.definition: Earning bitcoin means selling a product or service and being paid in it.

nodes.label: Bitcoin ATM
nodes.body: A Bitcoin ATM is a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoins to your smartphone Bitcoin wallet, as the chapter defines it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The abbreviation ATM stands for automated teller machine, the cash machines of banks, and the Bitcoin version works in the other direction: it takes cash and pays out bitcoin.

paras.text: A Bitcoin ATM is a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoins to your smartphone Bitcoin wallet, as the chapter defines it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The abbreviation ATM stands for automated teller machine, the cash machines of banks, and the Bitcoin version works in the other direction: it takes cash and pays out bitcoin.

The ATM is the quickest route for a person who has cash and no friend with bitcoin. The chapter lists it as the third method of acquisition, and in the story Alice, over the next days, buys more bitcoin using an ATM and an exchange (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The method combines a physical machine in a city with a wallet on a phone.

A Bitcoin ATM is found in shops and public places in some cities. The user opens the receive screen of the wallet, scans the machine's code or shows his own, inserts cash, and the machine sends the corresponding amount to the address. The machine's price is set by the operator, following the exchange rate.

The machine needs an address to send to, so the wallet must be installed first; this is the same procedure as Alice's Receive screen with a QR code. The operator converts the cash into bitcoin at its own rate and sends a transaction, which the wallet sees as incoming and, after confirmation, as final. The process combines a cash payment, which is reversible only by a dispute with the operator, with a bitcoin transfer that is not reversible.

Convenience has its prices, which are set by the operator and may include a margin over the market rate, and identity rules of the country may require the user to identify himself at the machine. The chapter's remarks on identity and regulation, which are explained in the concept of identity verification, apply when the machine links the user's identity to an address.

nodes.definition: A Bitcoin ATM is a machine that accepts cash and sends bitcoin to a smartphone wallet.

nodes.label: Currency exchange
nodes.body: A currency exchange is a business that offers a market for buyers and sellers to swap bitcoins with local currency. The chapter lists it as the fourth method of acquisition: use a Bitcoin currency exchange linked to your bank account. It adds that many countries now have currency exchanges of this kind, and that exchange-rate listing services such as BitcoinAverage often show a list of Bitcoin exchanges for each currency (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A currency exchange is a business that offers a market for buyers and sellers to swap bitcoins with local currency. The chapter lists it as the fourth method of acquisition: use a Bitcoin currency exchange linked to your bank account. It adds that many countries now have currency exchanges of this kind, and that exchange-rate listing services such as BitcoinAverage often show a list of Bitcoin exchanges for each currency (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The exchange is the main bridge between the traditional banking system and Bitcoin. A person who wants a larger amount, or wants to sell bitcoin for the national currency, uses one. The chapter notes that where bitcoin touches traditional systems such as currency exchanges, national and international regulations often apply, and that in order to exchange bitcoin for your national currency you will often be required to provide proof of identity and banking information (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Exchanges also act as custodians, in the sense of the key-control group: the bitcoin a customer has bought often stays in an account at the exchange, under the exchange's keys, until it is withdrawn to the customer's own wallet. Until that withdrawal the customer holds a claim and not the coins, which is the distinction the chapter makes when it contrasts wallets with accounts held by third parties (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter also gives a reason of its own for keeping the two apart: once an address is attached to an identity, other transactions associated with it may become easy to identify and track, which is why many users maintain dedicated exchange accounts independent from their wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The user opens an account, passes the identity checks, links a bank account, deposits national currency, and buys bitcoin at the market price, which the exchange takes from its own market of offers. Withdrawing the bitcoin to a wallet that the user controls moves the funds from the exchange's custody to the user's. The price is the floating exchange rate of the market where the trade takes place.

An exchange that holds the user's funds is a custodian, with the risks of custody. The identity attached to the account can connect the user to the addresses he withdraws to, with consequences for privacy: the chapter warns that once an address is attached to an identity, other transactions associated with it may become easy to identify and track, including earlier ones (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: an exchange linked to a bank account
nodes.definition: A currency exchange is a market where buyers and sellers swap bitcoin and local currency, usually through a linked bank account.

nodes.label: Identity verification
nodes.body: Identity verification is the process by which a company checks who a customer is before it sells him bitcoin for a reversible payment. The chapter says that companies accepting traditional electronic payments in return for bitcoin usually require buyers to undergo identity verification and credit-worthiness checks, which may take several days or weeks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Identity verification is the process by which a company checks who a customer is before it sells him bitcoin for a reversible payment. The chapter says that companies accepting traditional electronic payments in return for bitcoin usually require buyers to undergo identity verification and credit-worthiness checks, which may take several days or weeks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The checks protect the seller from the risk created by the difference between payment systems. Card payments and bank transfers can be reversed, whereas the bitcoin that was sent cannot. Because of this, a new user cannot buy bitcoin instantly with a credit card, although, as the chapter says, with a bit of patience and creative thinking you won't need to (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The checks are met at exchanges and at some Bitcoin ATMs. The chapter notes that national and international regulations often apply where bitcoin touches traditional systems, and that to exchange bitcoin for your national currency you will often be required to provide proof of identity and banking information (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The company collects the documents and data, compares them against the customer, and decides whether to allow the purchase. Afterwards its records connect the person to the addresses that receive his bitcoin. The chapter explains the privacy consequence: once a Bitcoin address is attached to an identity, other associated Bitcoin transactions may also become easy to identify and track, including transactions made earlier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Identity verification applies only to the points of contact with the traditional system. The chapter observes that acquiring, holding and spending bitcoin does not require you to divulge sensitive and personally identifiable information to third parties when used correctly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and so a person who obtains bitcoin from a friend or by earning it does not go through the check. The consequence is not that the check is optional where the law requires it.

nodes.example: proof of identity at an exchange
nodes.definition: Identity verification is the check of a customer's identity and credit-worthiness that companies converting traditional payments into bitcoin usually require.

nodes.label: Foundations
nodes.body: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch stops to explain each of those words, so that a student who has not met them before can follow the later branches without guessing.

paras.text: The Foundations branch collects the general technical ideas that the rest of the chapter takes for granted. Chapter 1 of the textbook introduces Bitcoin through a story about Alice and Joe, and in doing so it uses words such as digital signature, private key, blockchain, node, protocol and QR code as if every reader already knew them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch stops to explain each of those words, so that a student who has not met them before can follow the later branches without guessing.

A technical text is only as clear as its vocabulary. Bitcoin is built from ideas of cryptography, of distributed computing and of ordinary internet engineering, and none of the three is new to the specialist while all of them are new to many beginners. Explaining them once and in one place also shows an important fact about the subject: Bitcoin invents very little vocabulary of its own and mostly combines established techniques in a new arrangement, which is how the chapter itself describes Nakamoto's contribution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The ideas appear throughout the chapter. A hash function is used by proof of work, by the checksum of a recovery code and by Hashcash; a digital signature is what makes a transaction valid; a block and a blockchain are the record that the whole network maintains; and a protocol, an API, a URI and a QR code are the means by which wallets talk to each other and to the people who use them. Each later explanation points back to the concept here.

The branch has four sections. The Cryptography section explains the mathematical tools: the hash function, the digital signature, public-key cryptography, the private key, entropy, the checksum, the keyed hash and key stretching. The Chain section explains the block, the blockchain, the timestamp and the node. The Computing section explains the everyday technology on which Bitcoin runs, from the internet and its protocols to databases and operating systems. The Threats section explains malware and phishing, the two attacks that the chapter warns about.

Two cautions apply to the whole branch. The explanations are introductions, and the later chapters of the textbook return to the same ideas in greater depth, so a student should treat the examples here as the smallest correct version of each idea and not as a complete treatment. The examples in this branch are also deliberately small, with tiny numbers, so that they can be computed by hand or in a few lines of Python; real Bitcoin uses far larger values and different algorithms for some of them, and the text says where this matters.

nodes.label: Cryptography
nodes.body: Cryptography is the science of transforming data so that its meaning is hidden, so that undetected alteration is prevented, or so that unauthorised use is prevented. The Internet Security Glossary describes it in these terms and adds that if the transformation is reversible, cryptography also deals with restoring the data (Shirey, 2007). The Mozilla glossary puts it more simply, as the science that studies how to encode and transmit messages securely, and adds that it tackles identification, authentication and data integrity as well as confidentiality (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026).

paras.text: Cryptography is the science of transforming data so that its meaning is hidden, so that undetected alteration is prevented, or so that unauthorised use is prevented. The Internet Security Glossary describes it in these terms and adds that if the transformation is reversible, cryptography also deals with restoring the data (Shirey, 2007). The Mozilla glossary puts it more simply, as the science that studies how to encode and transmit messages securely, and adds that it tackles identification, authentication and data integrity as well as confidentiality (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026).

Digital money has a problem that physical money does not have. A banknote is hard to copy because of its paper and its printing, but a digital file can be copied perfectly and without cost. Chapter 1 explains that cryptography takes the place of the special paper and inks: it provides the basis for trusting the legitimacy of a user's claim to value, and cryptographic digital signatures let a user prove ownership of a digital asset (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Without cryptography there would be no way to say who may spend which coin.

Cryptography is met every time a person uses a secure website, signs a document digitally, or opens a payment application. In Bitcoin it appears in eight forms that this section explains: the hash function that condenses data into a fingerprint, the digital signature that proves who authorised a transaction, the public-key cryptography that makes signatures possible, the private key that a wallet protects, the entropy that makes keys unpredictable, the checksum that detects typing errors, the keyed hash that binds a result to a secret, and the key stretching that makes guessing slow.

The eight concepts form a chain. A wallet begins with entropy, which is randomness that an attacker cannot predict. The randomness becomes a private key, from which a public key is derived. The wallet then signs data with the private key, and anyone can check the signature with the public key, using a hash function to condense the data first. A checksum protects the backup against mistakes; a keyed hash is the building block from which the slow derivation is made; and key stretching slows down an attacker who tries to guess the backup.

Cryptography is often imagined as secrecy alone, which is a mistake that this chapter corrects. Bitcoin transactions are public, and nothing in them is encrypted; the cryptography of Bitcoin is used to prove who authorised a payment and to make the record hard to alter, not to hide it. A second mistake is to think that cryptography is magic. Its security rests on mathematical assumptions and on correct use, and most real losses come from bad use, such as a weak password or a stolen backup, and not from a failure of the mathematics.

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.body: A hash function is a function that maps data of any length to a result of fixed length, called the hash or digest. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a function that maps an arbitrary, variable-length bit string into a fixed-length string and adds that, for most computing applications, any change to the input should produce a different result (Shirey, 2007). The chapter's glossary calls a hash a digital commitment to some binary input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), which expresses the same idea: the short result commits its author to exactly one input.

paras.text: A hash function is a function that maps data of any length to a result of fixed length, called the hash or digest. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a function that maps an arbitrary, variable-length bit string into a fixed-length string and adds that, for most computing applications, any change to the input should produce a different result (Shirey, 2007). The chapter's glossary calls a hash a digital commitment to some binary input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), which expresses the same idea: the short result commits its author to exactly one input.

A fixed-length fingerprint is valuable because it makes large things easy to compare and to refer to. Two files are the same if their hashes are the same, and a signature need only cover the short hash and not the whole file. The standard that defines the SHA-2 family explains that a good hash function is secure in two ways: it is computationally infeasible to find a message that corresponds to a given digest, or to find two different messages with the same digest (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). These properties are what proof of work and the linking of blocks rely on.

In this chapter the hash function appears in four places. Proof of work searches for an input whose SHA-256 hash begins with zeros, Hashcash did the same for email, the recovery code of a wallet carries a checksum taken from a hash, and a block commits to the previous block by containing its hash (Nakamoto, 2008) (Back, 2002) (Palatinus et al., 2013). Outside Bitcoin the same tools protect passwords, verify downloaded software and identify files.

SHA-256, the function used by Bitcoin, takes a message of any practical length and returns 256 bits, which are normally written as 64 hexadecimal digits. The standard's own test vector shows the result for the three letters abc, and the example reproduces it with Python's hashlib module: the hash of abc begins ba7816bf and ends 20015ad (Eastlake and Hansen, 2011). A change of a single letter produces a completely different result: the hashes of abc and abd differ in 122 of their 256 bits, which is close to the half that one expects of an unpredictable function.

A hash function is not encryption. Nothing is hidden, because the same input always gives the same output, and nothing can be recovered from the output, because many inputs share the same hash in principle and the function is designed to be hard to run backwards. A hash also does not authenticate by itself, since anyone can compute the hash of altered data; it becomes useful when it is signed, published in a trusted place, or buried in a chain of blocks. Finally, short or guessable inputs can be found by trying them one after another, so a hash of a weak password protects little.

nodes.definition: A hash function maps data of any length to a fixed-length fingerprint; SHA-256 produces 256 bits, and any change to the input gives a different result.

nodes.label: Digital signature
nodes.body: A digital signature is a value computed from a data object and a secret key, which lets any recipient verify where the data came from and that it has not been changed. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a value computed with a cryptographic algorithm and associated with a data object in such a way that any recipient of the data can use the signature to verify the data's origin and integrity (Shirey, 2007). A handwritten signature offers a loose version of the same promise on paper.

paras.text: A digital signature is a value computed from a data object and a secret key, which lets any recipient verify where the data came from and that it has not been changed. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a value computed with a cryptographic algorithm and associated with a data object in such a way that any recipient of the data can use the signature to verify the data's origin and integrity (Shirey, 2007). A handwritten signature offers a loose version of the same promise on paper.

A digital signature is what allows money to be spent without a bank. Chapter 1 explains that cryptographic digital signatures enable a user to sign a digital asset or a transaction, proving the ownership of that asset, and that with the appropriate architecture they can also be used to address the double-spend issue (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper defines the electronic coin as a chain of digital signatures, in which each owner transfers the coin to the next by signing (Nakamoto, 2008). Without signatures, anybody could write a transaction in anybody else's name.

Every Bitcoin transaction carries signatures: Joe's wallet signs the transaction that pays Alice with his private keys, and this tells the network that Joe has authorised the transfer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Outside Bitcoin, digital signatures protect software updates, secure web connections, electronic contracts and the verifiable credentials that the semantic bridge of this chapter describes (World Wide Web Consortium, 2025).

Signing uses a pair of related keys. The signer computes the signature from the data and the private key, and a verifier checks it with the public key, which anyone may know. The example uses a toy scheme with the tiny public numbers n = 3233 and e = 17 and the private number d = 2753, which the next two concepts explain: the message 65 is signed as 65 raised to the power d, taken modulo n, which gives 588, and the verification raises 588 to the power e and recovers 65. The recovered value is 65 and not 66, so a verifier who is told that the message was 66 rejects the signature. Real systems sign the hash of the data and use far larger numbers.

A valid signature proves that someone holding the private key signed this exact data; it does not prove who that someone is, or that the signer meant well. If the private key is stolen, the thief can sign as the owner, and no one can tell the difference. A signature also covers only the data that was signed: a transaction that is changed after signing no longer verifies, but a transaction that was signed in error remains valid. The toy numbers of the example are far too small to be secure, and Bitcoin does not use this scheme; later chapters of the textbook explain the algorithm that it does use.

nodes.example: a toy signature with tiny numbers
nodes.definition: A digital signature is a value computed from data and a private key that anyone holding the matching public key can use to verify the origin and integrity of the data.

io.code: (lambda n, e, d, m: (pow(m, d, n), pow(pow(m, d, n), e, n) == m, pow(pow(m, d, n), e, n) == 66))(3233, 17, 2753, 65)

nodes.label: Public-key cryptography
nodes.body: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is cryptography in which each user has a pair of mathematically related keys. The Internet Security Glossary defines the public key as the publicly disclosable component of the pair and the private key as the secret component, and it describes the key pair as a set of related keys that is generated in a way that makes it computationally infeasible to derive the private key from knowledge of the public key (Shirey, 2007).

paras.text: Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is cryptography in which each user has a pair of mathematically related keys. The Internet Security Glossary defines the public key as the publicly disclosable component of the pair and the private key as the secret component, and it describes the key pair as a set of related keys that is generated in a way that makes it computationally infeasible to derive the private key from knowledge of the public key (Shirey, 2007).

Before public-key cryptography, two people who wanted to exchange secret or authenticated messages first had to share a secret key in some safe way, which does not work between strangers on the internet. With a key pair, the public half can be published to everybody, and only the private half has to be protected. This asymmetry is what makes it possible to prove ownership without revealing the secret, which is exactly what a payment system between strangers needs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Public-key cryptography is used in secure web connections, in signed email and software, and in Bitcoin. A Bitcoin wallet generates a private key, derives from it the public data that others see, and uses the pair to sign transactions, as chapter 1 describes when it says that Alice's wallet randomly generated a private key that is used to derive Bitcoin addresses (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The W3C identity standards of the semantic bridge rely on the same technique (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

The example uses a classic textbook construction with tiny numbers. Two small primes, 61 and 53, give n = 61 * 53 = 3233, and the public exponent e = 17 and the private exponent d = 2753 are chosen so that 17 * 2753 leaves the remainder 1 when divided by 60 * 52 = 3120. A message m = 65 is transformed with the public key as pow(65, 17, 3233), and the private key undoes the transformation: pow(that result, 2753, 3233) returns 65. Used in the other direction, the same pair produces and verifies signatures, as the previous concept shows.

The security of such a scheme depends on the difficulty of one mathematical problem, which for the toy numbers is trivial: anybody can split 3233 into its two factors and recompute the private key. Real keys use numbers that are hundreds of digits long, and Bitcoin uses a different mathematical construction altogether, which later chapters explain. A further caution is that the public key is public only in the sense that it may be shared; it must still be authentic, because an attacker who can substitute his own public key for yours receives what was meant for you.

nodes.example: a key pair with tiny numbers
nodes.definition: Public-key cryptography uses a pair of mathematically related keys, one public and one private, so that what one key does only the other can undo.

nodes.label: Private key
nodes.body: A private key is the secret component of a pair of cryptographic keys. The Internet Security Glossary describes it as the key that is known only by its user and used for asymmetric cryptography (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin the glossary of the textbook calls it the secret number that unlocks bitcoin sent to the corresponding address, and chapter 1 compares private keys to very long PINs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A private key is the secret component of a pair of cryptographic keys. The Internet Security Glossary describes it as the key that is known only by its user and used for asymmetric cryptography (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin the glossary of the textbook calls it the secret number that unlocks bitcoin sent to the corresponding address, and chapter 1 compares private keys to very long PINs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The private key is the only thing that a Bitcoin user must protect, because possession of the key that can sign a transaction is the only prerequisite to spending bitcoin (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is why the control of the key decides who owns the money: whoever holds the key controls the funds, and nobody else, not even the network, can stop them. The slogan of the chapter, your keys, your coins, is a statement about the private key.

Private keys live inside wallets. A noncustodial wallet generates them on the user's device and keeps them there, a hardware signing device keeps them inside special-purpose hardware, and a custodian keeps them for its customers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The recovery code of a wallet is a compact way of storing the information from which all of its private keys can be rebuilt.

A private key is a number chosen at random from an enormous range. The textbook's chapter on keys explains that a wallet obtains 256 bits of entropy from a random number generator and uses them to form a 256-bit number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A number of 256 bits can take 2 to the power 256 values, a figure with 78 decimal digits, which is far too many for anybody to try one after another. The wallet then derives the public data from the private key in a way that cannot be reversed in practice.

A private key must never be revealed, copied carelessly or typed into a page that asks for it. Anyone who sees it can spend the funds, and nothing can reverse the theft, since Bitcoin transactions are irreversible. The opposite danger is loss: a key that is destroyed without a backup takes the funds with it. Because of both dangers the chapter pairs the idea of control with the duty of backup, and it warns that applications which ask for the recovery code at unexpected moments may be fraudulent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: A private key is the secret half of a key pair; in Bitcoin it is a very large number whose holder alone can sign transactions that spend the corresponding bitcoin.

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.body: In cryptography, entropy is a measure of how unpredictable a secret is. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as an information-theoretic measure, usually stated as a number of bits, of the amount of uncertainty that an attacker faces to determine the value of a secret (Shirey, 2007). A secret with 20 bits of entropy is as hard to guess as a number chosen uniformly from about a million possibilities.

paras.text: In cryptography, entropy is a measure of how unpredictable a secret is. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as an information-theoretic measure, usually stated as a number of bits, of the amount of uncertainty that an attacker faces to determine the value of a secret (Shirey, 2007). A secret with 20 bits of entropy is as hard to guess as a number chosen uniformly from about a million possibilities.

A key is only as secret as the randomness behind it. If a wallet chose its keys in a predictable way, for example from the time of day, an attacker could try the likely values and find them. Chapter 1 therefore insists that the recovery code consists of numbers, letters or words selected randomly by the software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and the standard behind the word lists says that the sentence must encode entropy in a multiple of 32 bits (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Entropy appears when a wallet is created and whenever a recovery code is generated. BIP 39 calls the random bits at the start of the process the initial entropy and allows 128 to 256 bits of it, which gives sentences of 12 to 24 words (Palatinus et al., 2013). Operating systems provide random number generators for this purpose, and hardware signing devices include their own.

The BIP 39 recovery code turns entropy into words. Each word is chosen from a list of 2048 words, so each word carries 11 bits, because 2 to the power 11 is 2048. A sentence of 12 words therefore carries 12 * 11 = 132 bits, which are the 128 bits of initial entropy plus a 4-bit checksum, as the next concept explains. The number of bits, not the number of words, measures the security.

Entropy cannot be seen in the result, since a predictable secret may look as random as a good one. A recovery code that the user made up, or that came from a source of poor randomness, is far weaker than its length suggests, which is why the standard states that it is not a way to process user-created sentences into a wallet seed (Palatinus et al., 2013). A second caution is that entropy is used up by disclosure: a recovery code that was photographed or stored online is no longer secret, however many bits it carries.

nodes.definition: Entropy is a measure of unpredictability, counted in bits; a wallet needs enough of it that nobody can guess the key or recovery code.

nodes.label: Checksum
nodes.body: A checksum is a value that is computed from the contents of a data object and is stored or transmitted together with the object, so that changes in the data can be detected. This is the definition of the Internet Security Glossary (Shirey, 2007). A familiar example is the final check digit of a long number, which lets a machine notice that a digit was mistyped.

paras.text: A checksum is a value that is computed from the contents of a data object and is stored or transmitted together with the object, so that changes in the data can be detected. This is the definition of the Internet Security Glossary (Shirey, 2007). A familiar example is the final check digit of a long number, which lets a machine notice that a digit was mistyped.

People make mistakes when they copy a long secret by hand, and in Bitcoin a mistake can be costly because nobody can restore a lost or wrongly recorded key. A checksum turns many such mistakes into an error message instead of a silent failure. The standard for recovery codes uses one for exactly this reason, and it also states its limit: the checksum is short, so it only gives modest odds of catching random errors, and it cannot help to correct them (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Checksums are found in credit card numbers, in barcodes, in file downloads and in the recovery codes of Bitcoin wallets. In BIP 39 a checksum is generated by taking the first ENT / 32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the initial entropy, where ENT is the length of the entropy in bits, and the checksum is appended to the entropy before the whole is divided into words (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The method is simple. The wallet computes the hash of the random bytes and keeps the first few bits. For 128 bits of entropy the checksum has 128 / 32 = 4 bits, and the example computes them for 16 bytes that are all zero: the first byte of their SHA-256 hash is shifted right by four places and leaves the value 3, which is the bit group 0011. A program that receives the words recomputes the hash of the entropy it decodes and compares the first bits; if they differ, it reports that the sentence is invalid.

A checksum detects accidental changes and does not defend against an attacker, who can recompute it after altering the data. It also does not tell where the error is. With 4 bits of checksum, one random error in 16 slips through unnoticed, and with 8 bits one in 256 does, which is the figure the standard gives (Palatinus et al., 2013). A checksum is therefore a convenience for honest users and not a form of security.

nodes.example: the first 4 bits of a SHA-256 hash
nodes.definition: A checksum is a short value computed from data and stored with it so that changes can be detected; a BIP 39 recovery code carries ENT/32 bits taken from a SHA-256 hash.

nodes.label: Keyed hash
nodes.body: A keyed hash is a hash that is computed from two things rather than one: the data and a secret key. The result is usually called a message authentication code, because it lets a receiver who knows the same key confirm both that the data is unaltered and that it came from someone holding the key. The construction that is used almost everywhere is called HMAC, which takes an ordinary hash function and a key and combines them in a fixed way; written as HMAC-SHA512, it means the construction applied with SHA-512 as the inner hash function.

paras.text: A keyed hash is a hash that is computed from two things rather than one: the data and a secret key. The result is usually called a message authentication code, because it lets a receiver who knows the same key confirm both that the data is unaltered and that it came from someone holding the key. The construction that is used almost everywhere is called HMAC, which takes an ordinary hash function and a key and combines them in a fixed way; written as HMAC-SHA512, it means the construction applied with SHA-512 as the inner hash function.

A plain hash proves nothing about who computed it, because anybody can hash anything, as the section on the hash function warns. Mixing in a secret repairs exactly that gap: a value that could only be produced by a holder of the key is evidence about the author and not only about the data. The same property has a second use, which is the one this chapter needs. If the key is the secret from which a wallet derives its keys, then the keyed hash is a function that nobody without the secret can compute, which is what a key derivation needs at its core.

A reader meets the keyed hash in the standard for recovery codes, which turns the words into a binary seed using the function PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512 as the underlying function and an iteration count of 2048 (Palatinus et al., 2013). Outside Bitcoin, keyed hashes protect session cookies, sign programming interface requests and authenticate messages on the network, and the standard that defines SHA also defines HMAC alongside it.

The construction pads the key to the block length of the hash function, combines it with two fixed byte patterns, and hashes twice: once over the first pattern and the message, and once over the second pattern and that intermediate result. The reader does not have to carry out those steps, because the standard library offers the whole construction: the example computes HMAC-SHA512 over the message with the key and finds that the result is 64 bytes long, the same 512 bits that the hash function alone would give. Only the length is public; the value itself depends on the key.

A keyed hash is not encryption, so the data it protects is not hidden, and it is not a digital signature, because the same key is needed to check the result as to produce it: a keyed hash convinces the two parties who share the key and nobody else, while a signature convinces everyone. The security also rests entirely on the key: a keyed hash computed with a guessable key is as weak as that key, which is why the next section's slow derivation exists.

nodes.definition: A keyed hash, or message authentication code, mixes a secret key into a hash so that only a holder of the key can produce or confirm the result; HMAC is the standard construction.

nodes.label: Key stretching
nodes.body: Key stretching is the use of a deliberately slow, repeated computation to derive a key from a secret. The standard for password-based cryptography describes the technique as including an iteration count in the key derivation, which indicates how many times to iterate some underlying function by which keys are derived (Moriarty et al., 2017). The function that BIP 39 uses is called PBKDF2, and it is defined in that standard.

paras.text: Key stretching is the use of a deliberately slow, repeated computation to derive a key from a secret. The standard for password-based cryptography describes the technique as including an iteration count in the key derivation, which indicates how many times to iterate some underlying function by which keys are derived (Moriarty et al., 2017). The function that BIP 39 uses is called PBKDF2, and it is defined in that standard.

Human-chosen or short secrets can be guessed by trying them one after another. If one guess costs a single fast computation, an attacker can try billions of them; if each guess costs thousands of repetitions, the attacker's work grows by the same factor while the honest user, who computes only once, hardly notices. The standard explains the reasoning: a modest number of iterations, say 1000, is not likely to be a burden for legitimate parties but will be a significant burden for opponents (Moriarty et al., 2017).

Key stretching is used wherever a key is made from a password or a phrase: in disk encryption, in password storage and in wallets. In the recovery code standard, the sentence of words is turned into a binary seed with the PBKDF2 function, using the sentence as the password and the word mnemonic, followed by an optional passphrase, as the salt; the iteration count is 2048 and the underlying function is HMAC-SHA512 (Palatinus et al., 2013).

PBKDF2 applies a pseudorandom function, which is a function whose output cannot be told apart from random bits without the key, and in this standard is the keyed hash of the previous concept, to the password and a salt, a public value that makes the work specific to this use, repeats the application the stated number of times, and combines the results into the derived key (Moriarty et al., 2017). The worked example builds that loop out of the keyed hash rather than calling a ready-made function, so that every step is visible: it applies HMAC-SHA512 to the password and the salt followed by the block number 1, then applies it 2047 more times to its own previous output, and combines all the results with the exclusive-or operation. With SHA-512 as the underlying hash function the derived key has 512 bits, which is 64 bytes, and for the word abandon with the salt mnemonic the first four bytes of the result are d96147bf.

Stretching raises the cost of guessing but does not remove it; a weak secret remains weak, only slower to attack. The iteration count of 2048 in the recovery code standard is modest by present standards, and the strength of the code comes mainly from the random entropy behind it and not from the stretching. The same words with the same passphrase always give the same seed, which is the feature that makes recovery possible and also the reason that the words must be guarded.

nodes.definition: Key stretching derives a key from a secret by repeating a function many times, so that every guess of an attacker costs as much work as the honest computation.

nodes.label: Chain
nodes.body: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network. The chapter uses all four words in its first pages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Chain section explains the data structure at the centre of Bitcoin and the computers that maintain it. The block is a group of transactions that the network accepts together, the blockchain is the list of blocks linked one to the next, the timestamp is the mark of time that orders them, and the node is a computer that takes part in the network. The chapter uses all four words in its first pages (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A payment system needs a single agreed record of what happened and in what order. In the system of a bank this record is a database that the bank keeps. In Bitcoin it is the blockchain, kept by thousands of nodes at once, with each block fixing the order of its transactions and tying itself to the past. Understanding the chain makes clear why changing an old payment is so hard.

The vocabulary of the chain appears throughout chapter 1: in the description of mining, which adds a block roughly every ten minutes; in the sidebar on confirmations, which counts blocks to decide when a payment may be trusted; and in the account of how Joe's transaction spreads from node to node until most of the well-connected nodes have it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same four words are used outside the book by block explorers, which display the chain, by wallets, which report a confirmation count, and by news reports, which quote block heights and times. A student who reads them in this course should expect to meet them again in every later chapter.

The four concepts are explained from the inside out. The block is the unit. The blockchain is the chain of units, tied together by hashes. The timestamp explains the time mark that each block carries and what it is good for. The node explains who stores and checks the chain, and prepares the later sections on full nodes and lightweight clients.

The word blockchain is used in many different senses in popular writing, where it often means any shared database with some cryptography in it. In this course it keeps the narrower sense of the textbook's glossary: the particular list of validated blocks that the Bitcoin network agrees on, each one linked to its predecessor back to the first block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word node is similarly narrowed, since the chapter uses it for a computer that takes part in this network and not for any point in any graph. Keeping the vocabulary this strict is what lets the later chapters make precise statements.

nodes.label: Block
nodes.body: A block is a group of transactions that the network accepts as one unit. The glossary of the textbook defines it as a grouping of transactions, marked with a timestamp, and a commitment to the previous block; its header is hashed to produce a proof of work, thereby validating the transactions, and valid blocks are added to the main blockchain by network consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block also contains one special first transaction that pays the miner's reward.

paras.text: A block is a group of transactions that the network accepts as one unit. The glossary of the textbook defines it as a grouping of transactions, marked with a timestamp, and a commitment to the previous block; its header is hashed to produce a proof of work, thereby validating the transactions, and valid blocks are added to the main blockchain by network consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block also contains one special first transaction that pays the miner's reward.

Blocks give the network a rhythm and an order. Transactions arrive continuously and in different orders at different nodes, so the network needs a periodic moment at which one set of transactions is fixed. The chapter explains that a transaction is confirmed when it is included in a block, which happens every 10 minutes on average and is called clearing in traditional financial terms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block is also the unit in which the reward is paid and the unit that proof of work protects.

Blocks are seen in every block explorer and every wallet that displays a confirmation count. The data of the first block, saved from the explorer of Blockstream, shows that it contains one transaction, whereas block 840000, in which the fourth halving took effect, contains 3050 transactions (Blockstream, 2026). The size of a block therefore varies with the demand for space, even though its rhythm is steady.

A miner collects waiting transactions, places a special reward transaction first, and builds a block header that contains, among other data, the hash of the previous block, a summary of the transactions and the time. The miner then searches for a header whose hash is small enough, which is the proof of work. Nodes that receive the block check the header, the transactions and the reward, and add the block to their chain only if all checks pass. The glossary adds that the first transaction is created by a miner and includes a single special field, which allows claiming the block reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A block is not a file of money; it records transfers, and the coins themselves are implied by those transfers. A block is also not final the moment it is found, because a rival block at the same height may win, so the transactions inside it gain certainty only as further blocks are added. The number of transactions in a block is not fixed, and the figures in the example are only two data points.

nodes.definition: A block is a group of transactions, marked with a time and committing to the previous block, that is added to the blockchain once it carries a valid proof of work.

nodes.label: Blockchain
nodes.body: The blockchain is the list of validated blocks in which each block links to its predecessor all the way back to the first block, which the glossary of the textbook calls the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 also uses the word for the transaction journal: a transaction is confirmed when it has been recorded in the Bitcoin transaction journal, known as the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper itself speaks of a chain of blocks and of the longest proof-of-work chain.

paras.text: The blockchain is the list of validated blocks in which each block links to its predecessor all the way back to the first block, which the glossary of the textbook calls the genesis block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 also uses the word for the transaction journal: a transaction is confirmed when it has been recorded in the Bitcoin transaction journal, known as the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The whitepaper itself speaks of a chain of blocks and of the longest proof-of-work chain.

Linking the blocks is what turns a pile of records into a history that is hard to rewrite. Each block contains the hash of the one before it, so changing an old block changes its hash, which no longer matches the link stored in the next block. The attacker would have to redo the proof of work for that block and for every block that follows. The whitepaper describes the rule that makes this decisive: nodes treat the longest chain, the one with the most work invested in it, as the correct one (Nakamoto, 2008).

The blockchain is stored by every full node, displayed by block explorers and quoted in news reports. The chapter's sidebar on digital currencies before Bitcoin explains why the structure was needed: earlier systems used a central clearinghouse, whereas Bitcoin keeps the public journal itself on a decentralized network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The example builds a toy chain in which each block is the SHA-256 hash of the previous hash joined with the block's data. The program creates three blocks, recomputes the chain to check it, and gets True; it then changes the data of the first block, recomputes, and finds that the stored hashes no longer match, which gives False. Bitcoin does the same with real block headers, and adds proof of work, so that rebuilding the chain after a change also costs an enormous amount of computation.

The blockchain is not secret, not encrypted, and not a database that a company controls; its entire content is public. It is also not a guarantee that its content is true: it proves that a transaction was recorded, not that the sale behind the transaction was honest. A final caution concerns the word itself, which is used loosely for any shared ledger; this course reserves it for the chain that the Bitcoin network maintains.

nodes.definition: The blockchain is the list of validated blocks, each linking to its predecessor all the way back to the first block; changing an old block breaks every later link.

nodes.label: Timestamp
nodes.body: A timestamp is a label that records the time at which a data object was marked. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a label or marking in which is recorded the time, of day or other instant of elapsed time, at which the label or marking was affixed to the data object (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin, the glossary of the textbook says that a block is marked with a timestamp (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A timestamp is a label that records the time at which a data object was marked. The Internet Security Glossary defines it as a label or marking in which is recorded the time, of day or other instant of elapsed time, at which the label or marking was affixed to the data object (Shirey, 2007). In Bitcoin, the glossary of the textbook says that a block is marked with a timestamp (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Time gives order, and order is the answer to the double-spend problem: when two transactions spend the same coin, the one that came first counts. The whitepaper builds its solution on this point and begins with a timestamp server, which takes a hash of a block of items to be timestamped and widely publishes the hash, proving that the data must have existed at that time (Nakamoto, 2008). Bitcoin replaces the trusted server by the network.

Timestamps are met in block explorers, in file systems and in digital certificates. Each Bitcoin block carries one; the block data of the first block shows the number 1231006505, which counts the seconds since the start of 1 January 1970 in universal time (Blockstream, 2026). Programs convert that number into a calendar date.

The number is a count of seconds, and the example converts it: 1231006505 seconds after the origin of the count is 2009-01-03 18:15:05 in universal time, the moment that the first block's header claims. A timestamp inside a block is set by the miner and is checked only roughly by the nodes, so it is accurate enough to order blocks and to adjust difficulty, but not to settle a dispute about a minute.

A timestamp does not prove that an event happened at that time, only that the data was marked then, and a miner can choose a time within the permitted limits. Block times are also averages: although the target is one block in 10 minutes, individual blocks can arrive seconds or hours apart, so a calendar prediction based on blocks, such as the date of a halving, is an estimate.

nodes.definition: A timestamp is a recorded time attached to data; each block carries one, and together they place the transactions in an agreed order.
