nodes.label: Node
nodes.body: A node is a computer that takes part in the Bitcoin network by running software that speaks its protocol. The textbook's chapter on the network defines the term Bitcoin network as the collection of nodes running the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol, and says that a Bitcoin full node validates blocks and may contain other functions, such as routing, mining and wallet services (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In everyday use the word means a full node unless something else is said.

paras.text: A node is a computer that takes part in the Bitcoin network by running software that speaks its protocol. The textbook's chapter on the network defines the term Bitcoin network as the collection of nodes running the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol, and says that a Bitcoin full node validates blocks and may contain other functions, such as routing, mining and wallet services (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In everyday use the word means a full node unless something else is said.

The network has no central server, so the nodes together do the work that a server would do. They receive transactions, check them, pass them on, and keep copies of the chain. Because anyone can run a node, the rules of Bitcoin are enforced by the participants and not by a company, and the more independent nodes there are, the harder it is for any party to change the rules by force.

In the chapter's story, the transaction that Joe's wallet sends spreads from node to node, and after just a few seconds most of the well-connected nodes in the network receive it and see Alice's address for the first time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nodes are run by individuals, companies and exchanges, in homes and data centres, on laptops and dedicated machines.

A node connects to several other nodes at random, asks them for the blocks it does not have, checks each block and each transaction against the rules, and relays what it accepts. The network chapter lists the roles a node can take: some keep a complete copy of the chain, some mine, and some offer wallet services (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A node is not a wallet and not a miner, although one program may play all three roles. A node is also not the same as a user: most users run lightweight wallets that depend on nodes. Finally, the number of nodes is not a measure of security by itself, since many nodes may be run by the same party; what matters is how independent they are.

nodes.definition: A node is a computer that takes part in the Bitcoin network and runs software that speaks its protocol; full nodes validate blocks and may also route, mine or serve wallets.

nodes.label: Computing
nodes.body: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it. It covers the internet and the rules that computers follow on it, the way programs talk to each other through interfaces, the way data is named and stored, the operating systems and browsers in which wallets live, and the units in which computers count. Chapter 1 mentions all of these in passing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Computing section explains the ordinary technology on which Bitcoin software runs and by which people reach it. It covers the internet and the rules that computers follow on it, the way programs talk to each other through interfaces, the way data is named and stored, the operating systems and browsers in which wallets live, and the units in which computers count. Chapter 1 mentions all of these in passing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin is software, and software is built on top of other software. A student who understands the layers beneath a wallet can see which parts of the system belong to Bitcoin and which belong to the general technology of computing. This also explains the chapter's comparison between wallets and web browsers: both are applications that speak a protocol on top of the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The terms appear when the chapter says that Bitcoin users communicate with each other using the Bitcoin protocol primarily via the internet, that a wallet is like a web browser for the HTTP protocol, that a desktop wallet runs on a general-use operating system, and that a mobile wallet retrieves information from remote servers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Later sections add the QR code, the URI of an invoice and the database in which a wallet keeps its labels.

The twelve concepts of the section move from the network to the machine. The internet, the protocol, HTTP, the server and the distributed system describe how computers cooperate. The API, the URI and the QR code describe how programs and people name and exchange things. The web browser, the operating system and the database describe where software runs and where data is kept. The bit and the byte describe how data is measured.

Each of these technologies is a large field of its own, and a few paragraphs cannot do any of them justice. The goal of this section is therefore deliberately modest: for each term, a working definition taken from a published glossary, the one fact about it that chapter 1 actually needs, a small example where one can be computed, and a warning about the misunderstanding that most often follows. A student who already knows these terms can read the section quickly; a student who does not should read it before the Wallet and Usage branches, which use the words without explanation.

nodes.label: Internet
nodes.body: The Internet is a worldwide network of networks that uses the Internet protocol suite, named TCP/IP after its two most important protocols (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as the single, interconnected, worldwide system of commercial, governmental, educational and other computer networks that share the protocol suite specified by the Internet Architecture Board (Shirey, 2007). The word is capitalised when it names this one network.

paras.text: The Internet is a worldwide network of networks that uses the Internet protocol suite, named TCP/IP after its two most important protocols (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as the single, interconnected, worldwide system of commercial, governmental, educational and other computer networks that share the protocol suite specified by the Internet Architecture Board (Shirey, 2007). The word is capitalised when it names this one network.

The Internet is the medium that carries nearly all Bitcoin traffic. The chapter says that Bitcoin users communicate with each other using the Bitcoin protocol primarily via the internet, although other transport networks can also be used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the Internet already connects billions of devices without a central operator of its own, a payment system for the internet could be built without asking anyone's permission.

Everyone meets the Internet through a device and a provider. In the chapter's story, Joe's transaction crosses it from his phone to the first nodes it can reach, and Alice's wallet listens to it for incoming payments (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The textbook's chapter on the network adds that Bitcoin is structured as a peer-to-peer network architecture on top of the internet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The Internet works by dividing every message into small packets that are forwarded from network to network until they arrive. No single machine controls the path. The rules that make this possible are protocols, which the next concept explains, and the higher-level protocols such as HTTP run on top of the lower ones.

The Internet is not the Web. The Web is one service that runs on the Internet, built from pages, links and the HTTP protocol, while email, file transfer and the Bitcoin network are other services that use the same medium. The Internet is also not private: messages cross machines owned by many parties, which is why sensitive data must be protected by cryptography.

nodes.definition: The Internet is a worldwide network of networks that uses the Internet protocol suite; Bitcoin users communicate over it primarily, although other transport networks can be used.

nodes.label: Protocol
nodes.body: A protocol is a system of rules that defines how data is exchanged within or between computers. The Mozilla glossary adds that communications between devices require that the devices agree on the format of the data, and that the set of rules that defines a format is called a protocol (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as a set of rules, meaning formats and procedures, to implement and control some type of association between systems, and gives the Internet Protocol as an example (Shirey, 2007).

paras.text: A protocol is a system of rules that defines how data is exchanged within or between computers. The Mozilla glossary adds that communications between devices require that the devices agree on the format of the data, and that the set of rules that defines a format is called a protocol (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as a set of rules, meaning formats and procedures, to implement and control some type of association between systems, and gives the Internet Protocol as an example (Shirey, 2007).

Computers made by different companies, running different programs, can cooperate only if they agree beforehand on the form of their messages. A protocol is that agreement. For Bitcoin, the protocol is what lets a wallet written by one team talk to a node written by another, and it is the reason that, as the chapter says, there are many implementations and brands of wallets, just as there are many brands of web browsers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Protocols are met at every layer of computing. The chapter speaks of the Bitcoin protocol, of the protocol stack that is available as open source software, and of the HTTP protocol of the web (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The textbook's chapter on the network adds that, besides the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol, other protocols are used for mining and lightweight wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A protocol defines who speaks first, what messages exist, how each message is laid out in bytes, and what each side must do when it receives one. A program that follows the rules is a correct implementation. The example uses a message of the web protocol, whose request line is made of three parts separated by single spaces, a method, a target and a version, and the program splits one such line into its three parts.

A protocol is a specification, not a program. Several programs can implement the same protocol, and they can differ in quality while still being compatible. In Bitcoin the written description of the protocol is incomplete, so the behaviour of the reference implementation has in practice served as the standard; this is why the idea of a reference implementation matters and why changes to the rules have to be coordinated.

nodes.definition: A protocol is a set of rules, formats and procedures that computers follow to exchange data; the Bitcoin protocol is the rules that nodes follow to talk to each other.

nodes.label: HTTP
nodes.body: HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the underlying network protocol that enables the transfer of hypermedia documents on the Web, typically between a browser and a server so that humans can read them (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). It is textual, which means that all communication is done in plain text, and stateless, which means that no communication is aware of previous communications.

paras.text: HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the underlying network protocol that enables the transfer of hypermedia documents on the Web, typically between a browser and a server so that humans can read them (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). It is textual, which means that all communication is done in plain text, and stateless, which means that no communication is aware of previous communications.

HTTP matters to this chapter because the textbook uses it as its model for the relationship between Bitcoin and its wallets: a Bitcoin wallet is the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just like a web browser is the most common user interface for the HTTP protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The analogy tells a student that the protocol is the stable standard and that applications on top of it compete on quality and convenience.

HTTP is the protocol of every website and, in the form of web services, of many programming interfaces. A wallet that obtains balances from a remote service usually does so over HTTP, and the identity standards at the end of the chapter use web addresses that begin with the scheme http or https (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The secure variant, https, carries the same messages through an encrypted channel.

A client opens a connection to a server and sends a request. The standard for the message syntax says that a request begins with a request line made of a method, a request target and the protocol version, each separated by a single space (Fielding et al., 2022). The example splits the line GET /index.html HTTP/1.1 into those three parts, and the server replies with a status and, normally, a document.

HTTP by itself provides no confidentiality: unless the https variant is used, anybody on the path can read the messages. Statelessness also means that a server does not remember a visitor between requests unless the application adds a mechanism for that. Finally, a page in a browser looks the same whether its data is stored on the user's device or on the provider's server, which is the confusion that makes web wallets risky.

nodes.example: a request line of the web protocol
nodes.definition: HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol, is the network protocol by which browsers and servers exchange web pages; its requests are plain text.

nodes.label: Web browser
nodes.body: A web browser, or browser, is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users reach further pages through hyperlinks (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The same glossary adds two details that explain what the program really is: a browser is the most familiar type of user agent, that is, a program acting on a person's behalf when it speaks to a server, and it uses a rendering engine to display the pages it fetches (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The chapter names three well-known examples, Chrome, Safari and Firefox, when it compares Bitcoin wallets with browsers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A web browser, or browser, is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users reach further pages through hyperlinks (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The same glossary adds two details that explain what the program really is: a browser is the most familiar type of user agent, that is, a program acting on a person's behalf when it speaks to a server, and it uses a rendering engine to display the pages it fetches (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The chapter names three well-known examples, Chrome, Safari and Firefox, when it compares Bitcoin wallets with browsers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The browser is the everyday case of an application that makes a protocol usable by people. The chapter draws the comparison explicitly: a Bitcoin wallet is the most common user interface to the Bitcoin system, just like a web browser is the most common user interface for the HTTP protocol, and just as we all have our favourite browsers, wallets vary in quality, performance, security, privacy and reliability (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A browser is also a place where wallets live. The chapter describes the web wallet as one that is accessed through a web browser and stores the user's wallet on a server owned by a third party, similar to webmail, and notes that some such services run client-side code in the user's browser, which keeps control of the keys in the user's hands (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The browser sends requests by HTTP to a server, receives the page, and shows it. Code that arrives with the page can run inside the browser, in the user's own machine, and this is what the chapter means by client-side code. Whether the keys are generated and kept in the browser or on the provider's server decides who controls the funds.

Running in a browser makes a wallet easy to use and also exposes it to the risks of the web: a counterfeit page, a malicious extension, or a compromised provider. A student should therefore treat the address bar, and not the appearance of a page, as the evidence of where the page comes from.

nodes.example: the browsers Chrome, Safari and Firefox
nodes.definition: A web browser is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users reach further pages through links.

nodes.label: Server
nodes.body: A server is a software or hardware system that offers a service to a user, usually called a client (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary defines a client as a system entity that requests and uses a service provided by another system entity, called a server, and a server as an entity that provides a service in response to requests from clients (Shirey, 2007). A hardware server is a shared computer on a network, and a software server is a program that provides services to client programs.

paras.text: A server is a software or hardware system that offers a service to a user, usually called a client (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary defines a client as a system entity that requests and uses a service provided by another system entity, called a server, and a server as an entity that provides a service in response to requests from clients (Shirey, 2007). A hardware server is a shared computer on a network, and a software server is a program that provides services to client programs.

The server is the foundation of the usual internet service: one party runs the machine and everyone else depends on it. Chapter 1 contrasts this with Bitcoin, which it describes as a distributed, peer-to-peer system with no central server or point of control (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The contrast explains the design of the system: with no central server there is no single point to attack, to corrupt or to switch off.

Servers appear in the chapter wherever a third party is trusted. Most mobile wallets retrieve information from remote servers, which reduces privacy by disclosing addresses and balances; a web wallet stores the user's wallet on a server owned by a third party; and a third-party API client trusts the remote server to provide accurate information (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A client program connects to a server by a protocol, sends a request and receives a reply. The Mozilla glossary notes that the two traditionally connect by passing messages encoded using a protocol over an API, and gives the example of a web server sending a page to a browser (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). In a peer-to-peer network the roles are mixed, since the textbook's network chapter says that nodes both provide and consume services at the same time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A server is a role, not a kind of machine, and a powerful computer can be a client while a small one is a server. The word does not imply wrongdoing either; the point of the chapter is that depending on a server means trusting it, so that the user must decide how much trust each server has earned.

nodes.definition: A server is software or hardware that offers a service to clients over a network; Bitcoin's peer-to-peer design has no central server.

nodes.label: API
nodes.body: An API, an application programming interface, is a set of features and rules that exist inside a software program and enable interaction with it through software, as opposed to a human user interface. The Mozilla glossary describes it as a simple contract, the interface, between the application offering it and other items such as third-party software or hardware (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026).

paras.text: An API, an application programming interface, is a set of features and rules that exist inside a software program and enable interaction with it through software, as opposed to a human user interface. The Mozilla glossary describes it as a simple contract, the interface, between the application offering it and other items such as third-party software or hardware (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026).

A contract between programs lets each side change its inside without breaking the other, as long as the interface is kept. This is how large systems are built from parts made by different people. In the chapter, the idea appears in the third type of wallet: a third-party API client interacts with Bitcoin through a third-party system of APIs rather than by connecting to the Bitcoin network directly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

APIs are found in operating systems, in libraries and in web services. Python's standard library offers one: the hashlib module promises that the name sha256 is available on every platform, and the example confirms that the name appears in its list of algorithms that are guaranteed to be there. Web services of exchanges and of block explorers offer APIs that wallets call over HTTP (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026).

An API names the operations that may be requested, such as asking for the balance of an address, the form of each request and the form of each answer. The calling program sends a request, usually over HTTP, and receives a reply that it can process. It does not need to know how the answer was computed, which is both the convenience and the weakness of the arrangement.

A program that relies on an API trusts the service behind it to answer truthfully and to protect the privacy of the questions, which is why the chapter describes the third-party API client as trusting the remote server to provide it with accurate information and protect its privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An API can also change or disappear without notice, leaving applications that depend on it unable to work.

nodes.example: the interface a program offers to other programs
nodes.definition: An API is a set of features and rules by which software interacts with other software; a third-party API client uses a remote system's API instead of the Bitcoin network.

nodes.label: URI
nodes.body: A URI, a Uniform Resource Identifier, is a string that refers to a resource. The Mozilla glossary notes that the most common are URLs, which identify a resource by giving its location on the Web, whereas URNs refer to a resource by a name, such as the ISBN of a book (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The standard that defines the syntax says that a URI provides a simple and extensible means for identifying a resource (Berners-Lee et al., 2005).

paras.text: A URI, a Uniform Resource Identifier, is a string that refers to a resource. The Mozilla glossary notes that the most common are URLs, which identify a resource by giving its location on the Web, whereas URNs refer to a resource by a name, such as the ISBN of a book (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). The standard that defines the syntax says that a URI provides a simple and extensible means for identifying a resource (Berners-Lee et al., 2005).

A common syntax lets different programs recognise the same kind of reference. Every web address is a URI, and so is the link on a payment request. The textbook's glossary defines BIP 21 as a proposal to improve the bitcoin uniform resource identifier scheme (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and the W3C Decentralized Identifiers are URIs too: each DID is a URI that associates a DID subject with a DID document (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022).

URIs are met in browsers, where every web address is one, in documents that refer to other documents, and in wallets. When a wallet shows a QR code for a payment, the code usually contains a URI that begins with bitcoin: followed by an address and optional parameters; the BIP 21 text gives the example bitcoin:175tWpb8K1S7NmH4Zx6rewF9WQrcZv245W?amount=20.3&label=Luke-Jr (Schneider and Corallo, 2012). The identity standards at the end of this chapter use the same syntax for a different purpose, because each Decentralized Identifier is itself a URI (World Wide Web Consortium, 2022). One form of string therefore serves a page on the web, a request for a payment and the name of a subject.

The generic syntax is a scheme, a colon, and then the rest: URI = scheme : hier-part [ ? query ] [ # fragment ] (Berners-Lee et al., 2005). In the bitcoin example, the scheme is bitcoin, the path is the address, and the query holds the parameters amount and label. The example splits the string with Python's urllib and prints the three parts.

A URI only names a resource; it does not prove who made it or whether the destination is honest. A payment link received from an untrusted source may contain an address that belongs to a thief, so the source of a URI matters as much as its content. BIP 21 has itself been superseded by a later proposal, which shows that even a convention that wallets follow can change (Schneider and Corallo, 2012).

nodes.definition: A URI, a Uniform Resource Identifier, is a string that refers to a resource; the bitcoin: scheme of BIP 21 writes an address, an amount and a label as a URI.

nodes.label: QR code
nodes.body: A QR code, short for quick-response code, is a type of two-dimensional matrix barcode, invented in 1994 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The chapter describes the code that Alice's wallet shows as the square with a pattern of black and white dots, serving as a form of barcode that contains the same information in a format that can be scanned by Joe's smartphone camera (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A QR code, short for quick-response code, is a type of two-dimensional matrix barcode, invented in 1994 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The chapter describes the code that Alice's wallet shows as the square with a pattern of black and white dots, serving as a form of barcode that contains the same information in a format that can be scanned by Joe's smartphone camera (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin addresses are long strings of letters and numbers, and a single mistaken character can make a payment go astray. The QR code removes the typing: the chapter shows Joe scanning Alice's code so that he does not have to type in her address, which is quite long (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The code can also carry more than an address, because an invoice is a QR-encoded URI with an amount and a description.

QR codes appear on the Receive screens of wallets, on printed invoices, at shop checkouts and on Bitcoin ATMs. The chapter notes that a Bitcoin ATM sends bitcoins to your smartphone wallet, and the usual way to tell the machine where to send them is to show the wallet's code to its camera (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A QR code is a square grid of dark and light modules. Its size is described by a version number: version 1 is 21 by 21 modules and each further version adds four modules to each side, so that version 40 is 177 by 177 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The example computes 21 + 4 * (v - 1) for versions 1 and 40. Error correction is built in, so that a code can still be read when part of it is dirty or damaged.

A QR code is only a container, and what it contains can be anything. A code stuck over a legitimate one at a shop or printed in a fake invoice may point to a thief's address, and the eye cannot tell the difference. The wallet's screen, which shows the address and amount that were decoded, is the place to check before pressing Send. Also, the chapter warns that any funds sent to the addresses in the book will be lost (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the square of black and white dots
nodes.definition: A QR code is a two-dimensional matrix barcode that a camera can read; wallets use it to hand over addresses and payment requests without typing.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.body: A database is a storage system that collects organised data, making it easier to search, structure and extend (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). Most databases for web development use the relational model and the language SQL, although some use other models. In the chapter the word describes the place where a wallet keeps what it knows.

paras.text: A database is a storage system that collects organised data, making it easier to search, structure and extend (Mozilla Developer Network, 2026). Most databases for web development use the relational model and the language SQL, although some use other models. In the chapter the word describes the place where a wallet keeps what it knows.

A wallet has more to remember than keys: it must record the transactions it has sent or received and the notes that its user has added. The chapter says that a recovery code can be used to rebuild the wallet database of all the onchain transactions that Alice has ever sent or received, but that it will not restore the labels she entered, and so it advises frequent backups of the wallet database for wallets that use offchain payments (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Databases are met in banks, in shops, behind websites and inside mobile applications, usually without the user noticing them. In the Bitcoin world a wallet application keeps its own database on the device, which holds the transactions it has seen and the labels its user has written, and the chapter's glossary even speaks of the first blockchain database, which Satoshi Nakamoto devised as part of the original implementation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter meets the word twice more: a recovery code rebuilds the wallet database of all the onchain transactions a user has sent or received, and applications that support offchain payments are told to back that database up often (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A relational database stores its data in tables of rows and columns and answers questions written in a query language, usually SQL, while other designs store documents or key-value pairs instead. Whatever the design, two operations recur: looking a record up by a key, which is fast because the system keeps an index, and scanning for the records that satisfy a condition. The example builds the smallest version of both on a table of two rows that pairs an address with a label: it looks the label Alice up by the key addr1 through an index built from the rows, it scans the rows for the label that belongs to addr2 and finds Joe, and it asks whether addr3 is present and gets False. A wallet does the same when it shows the name a user has given to a payment, and it reports nothing when the address was never labelled.

A database is a copy of data and can be lost with the device that holds it. It can also be damaged or tampered with, and its contents may reveal who the user pays. A blockchain is a particular kind of shared record and should not be confused with a database that one party controls and can change.

nodes.example: the wallet's own store of labels
nodes.definition: A database is a storage system that collects organized data so that it is easier to search, structure and extend; a wallet keeps its labels and history in one.

nodes.label: Operating system
nodes.body: An operating system is system software that manages the hardware and software resources of a computer and provides common services for the programs that run on it (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The second half of that definition is the part that matters here: programs do not talk to the screen, the disk or the network themselves, but ask the operating system to do it for them, and the operating system decides whether to allow each request. Every wallet in this chapter is such a program, whether it runs on a desktop computer or on a telephone.

paras.text: An operating system is system software that manages the hardware and software resources of a computer and provides common services for the programs that run on it (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The second half of that definition is the part that matters here: programs do not talk to the screen, the disk or the network themselves, but ask the operating system to do it for them, and the operating system decides whether to allow each request. Every wallet in this chapter is such a program, whether it runs on a desktop computer or on a telephone.

The operating system decides how well a wallet is protected, because everything the wallet stores and every key it uses passes through it. The chapter explains the consequence for desktop wallets: running on general-use operating systems such as Windows and macOS has certain security disadvantages, as these platforms are often insecure and poorly configured (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter names the operating systems of the two kinds of computer on which wallets run: Windows and macOS on desktops, and Apple iOS and Android on smartphones (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A hardware signing device has its own special-purpose firmware, the fixed program stored in the device itself, which is why it is less exposed than a general-purpose machine.

The operating system starts programs, gives each one memory and a share of the processor, keeps files on disk, and controls access to the network. A program that wants to open a file or a connection makes a request, and the operating system grants or refuses it. Security software and updates are installed on this layer, and so are programs that do harm.

A wallet cannot be safer than the system under it: malicious software that gains control of the operating system can read what the wallet displays and what the user types. For the same reason a device that is rarely updated or that runs unknown programs is a poor place to keep a large amount of bitcoin.

nodes.example: the systems Windows, macOS, iOS and Android
nodes.definition: An operating system is system software that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and provides common services to programs; wallets run on top of one.

nodes.label: Distributed system
nodes.body: A distributed system is a computer system whose inter-communicating components are located on different networked computers (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The components coordinate their actions by passing messages and appear to the user as a single system. Chapter 1 calls Bitcoin a distributed, peer-to-peer system, and also a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A distributed system is a computer system whose inter-communicating components are located on different networked computers (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The components coordinate their actions by passing messages and appear to the user as a single system. Chapter 1 calls Bitcoin a distributed, peer-to-peer system, and also a distributed computing innovation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Distribution brings advantages and a difficulty. Many machines can offer more capacity and survive the failure of some of them, but they must agree about what has happened even though messages arrive late, in different orders, or not at all. The chapter presents Satoshi Nakamoto's solution to this problem as a breakthrough in distributed computing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023), and its sidebar names the classical form of the problem, the Byzantine Generals' Problem.

Distributed systems are found in search engines, in online shops, in databases that span several data centres and in file-sharing networks, and the pattern is old enough that the early internet is itself an example. The textbook's chapter on the network names file sharing as the largest and most successful application of the peer-to-peer form besides Bitcoin and the internet itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 1 adds that Bitcoin is a distributed computing innovation and that its solution to agreement without a leader is a breakthrough in distributed computing, so the term is not decoration but the field in which the invention is placed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The computers of a distributed system exchange messages according to a protocol and keep their own copies of the data. When one computer receives a change, it checks it and forwards it to the others. Agreement is reached by a rule that every participant applies in the same way; in Bitcoin that rule is consensus, produced by proof of work.

A distributed system is not automatically a decentralized one. A bank may spread its database across several data centres and still remain a single organisation in control of the whole, whereas Bitcoin is distributed and decentralized at once because no single party controls the rules. The two words describe the location of the machines and the location of the control, and they should not be mixed up.

nodes.definition: A distributed system is a set of computers that communicate over a network and work together; Bitcoin is a distributed system with no central server.

nodes.label: Bits and bytes
nodes.body: A bit, a contraction of binary digit, is the smallest unit of information storage and has two possible values, usually written 0 and 1 (Shirey, 2007). A byte is a group of bits that is normally eight, and the Internet Security Glossary uses the word octet for a unit of exactly eight bits (Shirey, 2007). Larger quantities are counted in bytes, and sizes of keys and hashes are counted in bits.

paras.text: A bit, a contraction of binary digit, is the smallest unit of information storage and has two possible values, usually written 0 and 1 (Shirey, 2007). A byte is a group of bits that is normally eight, and the Internet Security Glossary uses the word octet for a unit of exactly eight bits (Shirey, 2007). Larger quantities are counted in bytes, and sizes of keys and hashes are counted in bits.

Bitcoin documents quote many sizes, such as a hash of 256 bits, a recovery code of 128 to 256 bits of entropy, or a block that holds a certain number of bytes. A student who confuses bits with bytes is out by a factor of eight. The textbook's chapter on keys is careful about the conversion, noting that 256 bits are shown as 64 hexadecimal digits, each of 4 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bits and bytes are met in file sizes, in network speeds and in cryptographic parameters. Hexadecimal, or base 16, is the notation in which hashes and keys are usually written: the standard for encodings describes the base 16 encoding as using sixteen symbols, the digits and the letters A to F, to represent a group of four bits (Josefsson, 2006).

Because each hexadecimal digit stands for four bits, two digits stand for one byte. A 256-bit hash is therefore 32 bytes, written as 64 hexadecimal digits. The example takes the SHA-256 hash of the empty message and prints the length of the hash in bytes, 32, and the length of its hexadecimal form, 64.

A hexadecimal string is only a way of writing the data; it is not a different kind of number or a form of encryption. Care is needed with prefixes and cases, because the same bytes can be written with capital or small letters, and with units, because kilobyte can mean 1000 or 1024 bytes depending on the author.

nodes.definition: A bit is a binary digit, a byte is eight bits, and a hexadecimal digit stands for four bits; a 256-bit hash is 32 bytes or 64 hexadecimal digits.

nodes.label: Threats
nodes.body: The Threats section explains two attacks that chapter 1 warns about by name or by description: malicious software that steals or destroys, and phishing, which tricks a person into handing over a secret. Both aim at the weakest part of the system, which is often not the cryptography but the person or the device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Threats section explains two attacks that chapter 1 warns about by name or by description: malicious software that steals or destroys, and phishing, which tricks a person into handing over a secret. Both aim at the weakest part of the system, which is often not the cryptography but the person or the device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Bitcoin shifts the responsibility for both attacks onto the user, which is why a chapter for beginners warns about them at all. A bank can reverse a fraudulent card payment and issue a new card, but nobody can reverse a Bitcoin transaction and nobody can restore a recovery code that a thief has copied, because the chapter's own rules make a payment irreversible and a key the only proof of ownership (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The loss is therefore final, and it is final at the moment of the mistake rather than after an investigation. Recognising the two attacks is for that reason part of the basic knowledge of anyone who holds keys, in the same way that recognising a counterfeit note belongs to handling cash.

The warning appears in the section on recovery codes, where the chapter says that many malware applications mimic the design of a wallet, insist that you enter your recovery code, and relay it to the developer so that they can steal your funds, which is the equivalent of phishing websites (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same threats appear in the discussion of web wallets and desktop wallets.

The two concepts of the section describe the means and the method, and they usually appear together. Malware is the software that does the harm once it is running on a device: it can read files, watch what is typed, and send what it finds away. Phishing is the deception that persuades a person to install that software, to open a counterfeit page, or simply to type a secret where the attacker can read it. The chapter's own example joins the two in a single sentence, because the fake wallet application is malware that works by phishing: it imitates a real wallet and insists that the user enter the recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

No technology removes these threats completely, because both of them end at a decision that a person makes. The best defences are therefore habits rather than products: obtaining a wallet only from its official source, checking the publisher of an application and not only its name, never entering a recovery code except during the first set-up and a genuine recovery, as the chapter's rule says, and reading the address of a page before typing anything into it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second habit limits the damage when the first one fails, which is to keep only a small amount on a device that is used for everything else. The chapter's final piece of advice for an unexpected request is to consult an expert rather than to decide alone (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Malware
nodes.body: Malware, a contraction of malicious software, is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption or destruction to a computer, server, client or computer network, to leak private information, or to gain unauthorised access to information or systems (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary lists the word as a contraction of malicious software and discourages it as slang for the more formal term malicious logic (Shirey, 2007).

paras.text: Malware, a contraction of malicious software, is any software intentionally designed to cause disruption or destruction to a computer, server, client or computer network, to leak private information, or to gain unauthorised access to information or systems (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary lists the word as a contraction of malicious software and discourages it as slang for the more formal term malicious logic (Shirey, 2007).

Malware matters for Bitcoin because the money is protected only by a secret on the user's device. A program that can read that secret, or that can trick the user into typing it, can empty the wallet in seconds, and the result cannot be undone. The chapter warns that desktop operating systems are often insecure and poorly configured, which makes them attractive targets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter's example is malware that imitates a wallet: there are many malware applications that mimic the design of a wallet, insist that you enter your recovery code, and then relay the code to the malware developer so that they can steal your funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Other forms attack the clipboard, replace a copied address with the thief's, or log what the user types.

Malware reaches a device through a downloaded file, an application that looks legitimate, a malicious attachment or a weakness in the system. Once it runs it has the rights of the user, and it can read files, watch the keyboard, change what is displayed or send data away. A hardware signing device defends against this by keeping the key inside special hardware, which the chapter says makes such wallets less vulnerable to many types of attacks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Antivirus software lowers the risk but cannot remove it. A user should obtain wallets only from their official sources, keep the system up to date, and never keep a large amount of bitcoin on a device that is used for everything. Fake wallet applications often copy the name and the picture of a real one, so the publisher of an application should be checked as well as its name.

nodes.example: an application that imitates a wallet
nodes.definition: Malware is software intentionally designed to cause harm, to leak information or to gain unauthorised access; fake wallet applications are the chapter's example.

nodes.label: Phishing
nodes.body: Phishing is a form of social engineering and a scam in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing malware (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as a technique for attempting to acquire sensitive data, such as bank account numbers, through a fraudulent solicitation in email or on a website, in which the perpetrator masquerades as a legitimate business or reputable person (Shirey, 2007).

paras.text: Phishing is a form of social engineering and a scam in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing malware (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). The Internet Security Glossary describes it as a technique for attempting to acquire sensitive data, such as bank account numbers, through a fraudulent solicitation in email or on a website, in which the perpetrator masquerades as a legitimate business or reputable person (Shirey, 2007).

Phishing works because it attacks the person and not the machine. A perfect cryptographic system cannot help a user who gives the secret to someone who asks politely. The chapter makes the point with the recovery code: the application insists that you enter it, and the attacker then relays it to steal your funds, which it calls the equivalent of phishing websites that try to trick you into giving them your bank passphrase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Phishing is met in emails that claim to come from an exchange, in counterfeit websites with a similar address, in messages that offer free bitcoin, and in applications that imitate wallets. The chapter's rule for recovery codes is a defence against it: for most wallet applications, the only times they will ask for your recovery code are during the initial set-up, before you have received any bitcoins, and during recovery, after you have lost access to your original wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The attacker builds something that looks trustworthy and invents a reason for urgency, such as a locked account or a problem with the wallet. The victim types the secret into the attacker's page or application, and the attacker uses it at once. The chapter's advice for an unexpected request is to consult an expert to ensure you are not being phished (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A message can look entirely genuine, with correct logos and language, so appearance is not a test. The test is the situation: a recovery code is never needed outside set-up and recovery, and a request for it at any other time should be refused. Because Bitcoin payments are irreversible, there is no second chance after the secret has been given away.

nodes.example: a page that asks for the recovery code
nodes.definition: Phishing is a scam in which attackers deceive people into revealing sensitive information or installing malware; a wallet that asks for the recovery code at an unexpected time is a warning sign.

nodes.label: Nature
nodes.body: The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers. The first describes the characteristics of the currency, which is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust. The second describes the architecture, which the chapter lists as four innovations brought together: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, a public transaction journal, a set of rules for validation and issuance, and a mechanism for reaching consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Nature branch answers a question that precedes all the others: what kind of thing is Bitcoin? Chapter 1 gives two complementary answers. The first describes the characteristics of the currency, which is virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust. The second describes the architecture, which the chapter lists as four innovations brought together: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, a public transaction journal, a set of rules for validation and issuance, and a mechanism for reaching consensus (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A student who knows only how to use a wallet knows what Bitcoin does and not why it is built as it is. The characteristics explain the goals, and the architecture explains how the goals are met. The sidebar on digital currencies before Bitcoin makes the link: earlier systems were centralized and easy to attack, so a decentralized digital currency was needed to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The characteristics appear in the opening paragraphs of the chapter, where Bitcoin is called arguably the perfect form of money for the internet because it is fast, secure and borderless, and where the currency is described as entirely virtual (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The architecture appears in the list of what Bitcoin consists of, and each item of that list is then explained in the Network branch and the Foundations branch.

The branch has two sections. The Characteristic section contains four concepts, virtual, borderless, decentralized and robust, each of which names a property that the chapter attributes to the currency. The Architecture section contains three concepts that correspond to three of the four innovations in the chapter's list: the peer-to-peer protocol, the public journal and the consensus rule set. The fourth innovation, the proof-of-work mechanism, has its own concept in the Network branch.

A list of attractive adjectives is not an argument. Each characteristic is a claim that can be examined, and each depends on conditions: a currency is borderless only where people can reach the network, decentralized only while control stays spread out, and robust only against the threats it was designed for. The branch should be read as an account of design goals, with the evidence supplied by the other branches.

nodes.label: Characteristic
nodes.body: The Characteristic section collects four properties that the chapter attributes to the bitcoin currency: it is virtual, it is borderless, it is decentralized, and it is robust. The first two come from the opening description of the currency, where Bitcoin is called arguably the perfect form of money for the internet because it is fast, secure and borderless, and the last two from the sidebar that explains why a decentralized digital currency was needed at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The four are properties of the thing itself and not of any program that uses it, which is why they sit in their own branch rather than among the wallets.

paras.text: The Characteristic section collects four properties that the chapter attributes to the bitcoin currency: it is virtual, it is borderless, it is decentralized, and it is robust. The first two come from the opening description of the currency, where Bitcoin is called arguably the perfect form of money for the internet because it is fast, secure and borderless, and the last two from the sidebar that explains why a decentralized digital currency was needed at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The four are properties of the thing itself and not of any program that uses it, which is why they sit in their own branch rather than among the wallets.

These properties distinguish Bitcoin from conventional money and from the earlier digital currencies that the chapter's sidebar describes. Conventional money exists in a physical and an electronic form at once and is controlled by central institutions; the earlier digital currencies were electronic but centralized, and the sidebar records that they were therefore easy to attack and that most were litigated out of existence or collapsed with the company behind them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin combines a purely virtual existence with the absence of any central authority, and the chapter presents that combination, rather than either half of it, as the reason the currency suits the internet.

Each concept in the section is defined by the sentence of the chapter that introduces it and is then connected to the mechanism that makes it true, because a property without a mechanism is only a slogan. Virtual is shown by computing a balance from a list of transfers, which demonstrates that the coins need not exist anywhere as objects. Borderless, decentralized and robust are referred to the mechanisms of the other branches: the peer-to-peer protocol carries a payment without asking where its parties live, the consensus rules let every participant check issuance for himself, and proof of work makes the rewriting of history expensive. A learner who can name the mechanism for each property has understood the section.

nodes.label: Virtual
nodes.body: To say that the bitcoin currency is virtual is to say that it has no physical or object form. The chapter states this precisely: unlike traditional currencies, the bitcoin currency is entirely virtual, there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins, and the coins are implied in transactions that transfer value from spender to receiver (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: To say that the bitcoin currency is virtual is to say that it has no physical or object form. The chapter states this precisely: unlike traditional currencies, the bitcoin currency is entirely virtual, there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins, and the coins are implied in transactions that transfer value from spender to receiver (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The statement removes a common picture. Many people imagine a bitcoin as a file or a token that moves from one wallet to another, but nothing moves; the record of transfers is all there is. This is why the central question of the system is who may create a valid transfer, which the chapter answers by the control of keys: users control keys that allow them to prove ownership, and with these keys they sign transactions to unlock the value and spend it by transferring it to a new owner (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The property shows in every wallet. The balance that Alice sees is not a number stored somewhere as a coin; it is a figure that her wallet calculates from the transactions that involve her addresses. Alice's wallet shows 0.001 BTC as incoming as soon as it sees Joe's transaction, even though no coin has been delivered in the physical sense (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The example represents a tiny history as a list of transfers, Joe pays Alice 100000 satoshis, Alice pays Eve 30000, and Joe pays Eve 5000. The program computes each person's balance by adding what they received and subtracting what they sent: Alice has 70000 and Eve has 35000. No coin exists in the program, only the list. Bitcoin works on the same principle, with the list made public and validated by the nodes.

Virtual does not mean unreal. The value is real because people accept it, in the same way that the value of a bank balance is real. It also does not mean that nothing can be lost, since a lost key makes the funds unspendable. Finally, the word does not describe the system as a whole: the network, the miners and the wallets are physical machines that use real electricity and real hardware.

nodes.definition: The bitcoin currency is entirely virtual: there are no physical coins or even individual digital coins, only transactions that imply the coins.

nodes.label: Borderless
nodes.body: Borderless means that the currency is not tied to any country or to its financial institutions. The chapter says that Bitcoin is arguably the perfect form of money for the internet because it is fast, secure and borderless (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment is sent to an address and does not depend on the nationality of the recipient.

paras.text: Borderless means that the currency is not tied to any country or to its financial institutions. The chapter says that Bitcoin is arguably the perfect form of money for the internet because it is fast, secure and borderless (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment is sent to an address and does not depend on the nationality of the recipient.

Conventional payments between countries pass through banks and clearing systems that apply different rules and take time. The internet itself has no such borders, which is why a money that behaves like an internet service fits it so well. The chapter's list of what users can do is long: Bitcoin can be used to buy and sell goods, send money to people or organisations, or extend credit, just as with conventional currencies (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The property is met in remittances sent home across a border, in online purchases from a foreign seller, and in the global markets where bitcoin is exchanged for other currencies; the chapter notes that bitcoin can be purchased, sold and exchanged for other currencies at specialised currency exchanges (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also met in the reach of the software itself, since the protocol stack is open source and runs on a wide range of devices, including laptops and smartphones, which the chapter gives as the reason the technology is easily accessible (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payment to an address therefore looks the same to the network whether the payee is in the next street or on another continent.

Bitcoin is borderless because the network is a peer-to-peer system on top of the internet and the rules are the same everywhere. Anyone can run the software on a laptop or a smartphone, as the chapter notes, and any participant can send to any address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Where bitcoin touches the traditional system, at exchanges for example, national and international regulations often apply.

Borderless does not mean that law does not apply. The chapter states that national and international regulations often apply where bitcoin touches traditional systems, and that exchanging bitcoin for national currency will often require proof of identity and banking information (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word also says nothing about prices, which float and can differ from market to market.

nodes.definition: Bitcoin is fast, secure and borderless, which the chapter gives as the reason that it is arguably the perfect form of money for the internet.

nodes.label: Decentralized
nodes.body: A decentralized system is one that has no central authority or point of control. The chapter says that Bitcoin is decentralized by design, and free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its ordinary statement of the same idea is that there is no central server or point of control in the system.

paras.text: A decentralized system is one that has no central authority or point of control. The chapter says that Bitcoin is decentralized by design, and free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its ordinary statement of the same idea is that there is no central server or point of control in the system.

Centralization is a weakness of the systems that came before. The sidebar explains that earlier digital currencies worked but were centralized and, as a result, were easy to attack by governments and hackers; they used a central clearinghouse to settle all transactions, and most were litigated out of existence or collapsed when their parent company liquidated abruptly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Decentralization removes the single party whose failure or coercion would end the system.

The property appears in the way that Bitcoin is run. No one owns the network; the chapter states that neither Satoshi Nakamoto nor anyone else exerts individual control over the Bitcoin system, which operates based on fully transparent mathematical principles, open source code and consensus among participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Miners, nodes and wallet developers are separate parties.

Decentralization is achieved by spreading each function across many participants. Validation is done by every full node, issuance and clearing are done by miners competing for blocks, and the rules are written in software that everyone can read. The result is that no participant can unilaterally change a rule or block a payment; changing a rule requires nearly everyone to run new software.

Decentralization is a matter of degree and it can erode. If most of the mining were done by a few pools, or most users relied on a few custodians, the practical control would be concentrated, even though the design allows otherwise. The word also does not mean absence of rules: Bitcoin has strict rules, enforced by software instead of by a person.

nodes.definition: Bitcoin is decentralized by design and free of any central authority or point of control that can be attacked or corrupted.

nodes.label: Robust
nodes.body: Robust means able to withstand attack and interference and to keep working while under them. The chapter's sidebar states the requirement in one sentence: to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, a decentralized digital currency was needed to avoid a single point of attack (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two words of that sentence that a student should notice are antagonists, which covers both lawful and unlawful opponents, and single point of attack, which names what the design removes rather than what it adds.

paras.text: Robust means able to withstand attack and interference and to keep working while under them. The chapter's sidebar states the requirement in one sentence: to be robust against intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, a decentralized digital currency was needed to avoid a single point of attack (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The two words of that sentence that a student should notice are antagonists, which covers both lawful and unlawful opponents, and single point of attack, which names what the design removes rather than what it adds.

The history of digital money supplies the motive. The earlier projects were targeted by worried governments and were eventually litigated out of existence, or failed in spectacular crashes when the parent company liquidated abruptly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A currency intended to last must not depend on a company or an institution that can be pressured, sued or closed.

Robustness is a property of the whole design. The chapter points to mining as a security mechanism, noting that the number and power of the machines running the proof-of-work algorithm have increased exponentially, and that their combined computational power now exceeds the combined computing operations of the world's top supercomputers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The more work that protects the record, the harder it is to attack.

Robustness follows from decentralization plus cost. Because there is no central point, an attacker must act against many independent participants. Because the record is protected by proof of work, rewriting it would require repeating the work. The whitepaper expresses the resulting guarantee: as long as honest nodes control the majority of the computing power, the honest chain will grow the fastest and outpace any competing chains (Nakamoto, 2008).

Robust is not the same as invulnerable. The guarantee depends on the honest majority assumption, on the correctness of the software, and on users protecting their keys; the chapter itself lists dangers such as malware and phishing. A robust network can contain fragile wallets, and the weakest link is often the user's own device.

nodes.definition: A robust digital currency is built to withstand intervention by antagonists, whether legitimate governments or criminal elements, which a decentralized design makes possible.

nodes.label: Architecture
nodes.body: The Architecture section describes how the Bitcoin system is put together. After the opening pages, the chapter lists what Bitcoin consists of: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, a public transaction journal, a set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance, and a mechanism for reaching global decentralized consensus on the valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It adds that Bitcoin builds on decades of research in cryptography and distributed systems and includes at least four key innovations brought together in a unique and powerful combination.

paras.text: The Architecture section describes how the Bitcoin system is put together. After the opening pages, the chapter lists what Bitcoin consists of: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, a public transaction journal, a set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance, and a mechanism for reaching global decentralized consensus on the valid blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It adds that Bitcoin builds on decades of research in cryptography and distributed systems and includes at least four key innovations brought together in a unique and powerful combination.

The combination, rather than any single part, is the invention. Digital signatures, hash functions and peer-to-peer networks existed before. What was new was the arrangement in which they support each other, so that a money system works without a central party. A student who can name the four parts and say what each contributes understands the structure of the whole subject.

Three of the four parts are concepts of this section. The peer-to-peer protocol describes the network. The public journal describes the record. The consensus rule set describes the rules every participant applies. The fourth part, the proof-of-work mechanism, is explained in the Consensus section of the Network branch, because it is the means by which the other three are brought to agreement.

nodes.label: Peer-to-peer protocol
nodes.body: The peer-to-peer protocol is the first of the four parts of Bitcoin that the chapter lists: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, which it identifies as the Bitcoin protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The textbook's chapter on the network explains that the term peer-to-peer means that the full nodes that participate are peers to each other, that they can all perform the same functions, and that there are no special nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The peer-to-peer protocol is the first of the four parts of Bitcoin that the chapter lists: a decentralized peer-to-peer network, which it identifies as the Bitcoin protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The textbook's chapter on the network explains that the term peer-to-peer means that the full nodes that participate are peers to each other, that they can all perform the same functions, and that there are no special nodes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A peer-to-peer design removes the server. With no central machine to run, pay for, defend or shut down, the network has no single point of failure or control. The network chapter observes that peer-to-peer networks are inherently resilient, decentralized and open, and that decentralization of control is a core design principle of Bitcoin that can only be achieved and maintained by a flat and decentralized network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The network chapter describes the arrangement as a mesh with a flat topology, with no server, no centralized service and no hierarchy; nodes both provide and consume services at the same time. It also names file sharing as another large application of peer-to-peer technology (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the chapter's story, Joe's transaction reaches the whole network by being passed from peer to peer.

Each node connects to several others, and each message is passed on from node to node until it has reached everyone. The example models seven peers with a few links between them and floods a message from peer A; the program counts the rounds until every peer has it, and the answer is 4. The real network is far larger, but the principle is the same: reach grows with each round of forwarding.

Peer-to-peer does not mean that all participants are equal in practice. Many users run clients and not peers, as the chapter explains, and the network also contains gateway servers that extend it to other protocols (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A message passed from peer to peer is also not instantly delivered everywhere: it takes a few seconds for a transaction to reach most well-connected nodes.

nodes.definition: The Bitcoin protocol defines a decentralized peer-to-peer network in which every full node is a peer that both provides and consumes services.

nodes.label: Public journal
nodes.body: The public journal is the second part of Bitcoin in the chapter's list: a public transaction journal, the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A journal is a chronological record, and public means that anyone can read it. The chapter uses the same phrase when it explains confirmation, as the Bitcoin transaction journal known as the blockchain.

paras.text: The public journal is the second part of Bitcoin in the chapter's list: a public transaction journal, the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A journal is a chronological record, and public means that anyone can read it. The chapter uses the same phrase when it explains confirmation, as the Bitcoin transaction journal known as the blockchain.

A shared record is what lets strangers agree about who owns what without trusting one another. In a bank, only the bank sees the full ledger and the customers trust its statements. In Bitcoin the ledger is open, and every participant can check it, so trust is replaced by verification. The whitepaper makes the same argument: the only way to confirm the absence of a transaction is to be aware of all transactions, so the transactions must be publicly announced (Nakamoto, 2008).

The journal is met in block explorers, in the data that nodes download, and in the way wallets compute balances. The chapter tells us that Alice's address first shows Joe's payment as unconfirmed and that it is confirmed when it is recorded in the journal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The privacy consequence is also public: the chapter notes that once a Bitcoin address is attached to an identity, associated transactions may become easy to identify and track.

The journal is stored as a chain of blocks, each of which commits to its predecessor, and every full node keeps a copy. New entries are added by miners, in blocks, about every ten minutes, and each node checks them before appending them to its copy. The Chain section of the Foundations branch explains the structure in detail.

Public does not mean that the entries carry names. They carry addresses and amounts, which is pseudonymous and not anonymous, as the privacy concept of the Usage branch explains, and the whitepaper describes the same arrangement as keeping the public keys anonymous so that an amount can be seen moving without anything linking it to a person (Nakamoto, 2008). Nor does public mean complete: the journal holds only what was recorded on the chain, so payments made by the offchain methods of the Transfer group do not appear in it at all. A student should therefore read the journal as a record of onchain transfers between addresses and not as a list of who paid whom.

nodes.example: the blockchain as a public transaction journal
nodes.definition: The second part of Bitcoin is a public transaction journal, the blockchain, in which every confirmed transaction is recorded for anyone to read.

nodes.label: Consensus rule set
nodes.body: The consensus rule set is the third part of Bitcoin in the chapter's list: a set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance, which the chapter calls consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They define what makes a transaction valid, what makes a block valid, and how many new bitcoins a block may create.

paras.text: The consensus rule set is the third part of Bitcoin in the chapter's list: a set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance, which the chapter calls consensus rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). They define what makes a transaction valid, what makes a block valid, and how many new bitcoins a block may create.

Because Bitcoin has no referee, each participant must be able to decide for himself whether a transaction or a block is acceptable, and all of them must reach the same decision. The rules are the means of this. The chapter says that nobody can force you to accept any bitcoins that were created beyond the expected issuance rate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the rules make that statement true, because a block that breaks them is rejected.

The rules are written into the software of the nodes. Bitcoin Core's validation code, for instance, compares the amount that the first transaction of a block claims with the sum of the fees and the subsidy for the block height, and rejects the block if it claims more (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The difficulty and subsidy rules are in the same code.

Each node checks every block and every transaction against the rules before it accepts it. The example is a miniature of the reward rule: a block at height 840000 may claim at most the subsidy of 312,500,000 satoshis plus the fees. A claim of exactly the subsidy is accepted, a claim one satoshi higher is rejected, and a claim that includes 12,500,000 satoshis of fees is accepted.

The rules are valid only as long as the participants run them. Changing a rule means persuading nearly everyone to run new software, and a minority that runs different rules ends up on a chain of its own. A rule is also different from a policy that a single node applies for convenience, such as the fee below which it will not relay a transaction.

nodes.definition: The consensus rules are the set of rules for independent transaction validation and currency issuance that every participant applies in the same way.
